items.title: Apple Is Entering Its Slop Era
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
In an opinion piece for 404 Media, Matthew Gault argues that Apple has entered its "slop era," abandoning its reputation for innovative hardware in favor of recycled ideas and questionable design choices. Here's an excerpt: My ears perked up when I heard Apple's new foldable phones were cracking. I licked my lips when the company announced it's releasing a touch-screen laptop. This was a company that once charged $19 for a polishing cloth, asked $200 for a VESA mount, and sold $700 wheels for the Mac Pro. Now it's borrowing tired ideas from its competitors and launching hardware its previous leaders rejected.
 
The once dominant company is struggling to find its feet in an AI-driven post-Tim Cook world. John Ternus is the new CEO -- a 25 year veteran of the company with a track record of pushing harebrained hardware schemes like the much reviled Touch Bar and lawsuit inducing butterfly keyboard.
 
With Ternus at the helm, I feel there's a good chance Apple's best days are behind it, that it will have to make do with less, that it's declasse. Apple, blindsided by AI and relying on crowdpleasing hardware gimmicks, is downwardly mobile. It's in its slop era. The company that once asked consumers to "Think Different" is now releasing hardware that's just like everything else on the market.

items.title: Meta Settles Another Social Media Addiction Case Just Before Trial
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Meta has reached an undisclosed settlement in another social media addiction lawsuit, avoiding a trial scheduled for next month and leaving Snap as the sole remaining defendant. Engadget reports: The lawsuit was brought by an 18-year-old woman from Mississippi known as K.D.B who, according to Reuters, has "described staying awake for hours scrolling social media, losing focus in class and engaging in self-harm using methods shown in social media videos." Jury selection kicked off earlier this week in Los Angeles.
 
On Friday, K.D.B's lawyer announced that she had reached a settlement with Meta after previously settling with TikTok and YouTube. "We remain committed to improving safety for kids on social media apps and holding tech companies accountable, and we are pleased to have brought this matter to a just resolution on behalf of our client," attorney Emily Jeffcott said in a statement.
 
Now, Snap is the only remaining defendant in the case. CEO Evan Spiegel is expected to testify in the trial that could last several weeks. If he does take the stand, it will be the first time the Snap founder has appeared in a social media addiction trial. Snap previously settled in another high-profile case involving similar claims. A jury later ruled against Meta and YouTube in the trial and the two were ordered to pay $6 million in damages.

items.title: Anthropic VS code extension on Cursor backdoored for nearly 12 hours
items.author: Dan Goodin
items.content:
An official extension for Anthropic’s Claude model was backdoored and threatened as many as 5,000 developers' machines, multiple sources reported Friday. Anthropic so far has yet to warn customers of the incident.

The compromised package was a VS Code extension available in the marketplace of Cursor, a maker of AI-assisted developer tools, the company said Friday. The malicious version, 2.1.313, subsequently affected “at most 5,000 users,” presumably when they either downloaded it or their systems automatically fetched and installed it. Anthropic pushed version 2.1.314 several hours after the previous version became available on Cursor, according to independent researcher Kevin Beaumont. Both Beaumont and the CTO and co-founder of security firm Phorian said that version 2.1.313 was distributed through Anthropic’s official account on Cursor. So far, neither Cursor nor Anthropic has explained how the attackers gained control of the account.

In search of cloud credentials

“It was a supply-chain compromise where the attacker gained access to the official distribution channel,” Phorian CTO and co-founder Luke Roberts told Ars. “The malicious version 2.1.313 was posted to the official Anthropic account, effectively superseding 2.1.312. Extensions auto-update in Cursor by default, but users can configure this in settings.” Phorian has more details here.

items.title: Sam Altman Thinks Your PC Is Wasting Precious RAM
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
"Looks like OpenAI CEO Sam Altman wants to own all the computing resources and rent out terminals to the world as a way of propping up his business plan, now that debt-ridden AI companies are teetering on the edge," writes ancient Slashdot reader Gilmoure. Tom's Hardware reports: In an interview over beers with the YouTube channel Cheeky Pint, Altman said that local inference, and, by extension, people having DRAM in computers at home, is "quite terrible." When discussing local inference on home computers with open-source models, Altman discussed the assumption that people will be able to run local AI on their own computers, the ones they may already own or want to build.
 
Then he explained why that's a bad idea (at the 29-minute mark): "From a global allocation perspective, actually, it's quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world's limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used 5% of the time," Altman said. "You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you're trying to deal with this very supply-constrained environment. And somehow many people's intuition is the opposite of that."
 
While OpenAI does have some open-source models, its primary business is in closed-source models that run in data centers, so he's really defending the company's business model. OpenAI isn't exactly threatened by some laptops and gaming rigs just yet, but local AI could mean people one day paying less for subscriptions to models like GPT-6 Luna if they have the power to run them at home. Altman's talk suggests that the company would prefer that more RAM go to OpenAI's data centers rather than home computers, which also sparks enthusiast fears of not being able to own your own hardware or software, but rather rent an agent and a computer in the cloud.

items.title: Thousands of 'Ghost Students' Use AI to Steal Millions In Student Loans, DOJ Says
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
The Justice Department has charged five people in a crackdown on "ghost student" fraud, in which scammers allegedly use stolen identities and AI to enroll fake students in colleges, complete coursework, and collect federal student loan funds. Ars Technica reports: In a press release Thursday, the Department of Justice said it had uncovered a large-scale scheme relying partly on AI. The DOJ seized more than $750,000 in cryptocurrency from "a network associated with Kenyan nationals" after data analysis helped flag likely fraudsters. Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the DOJ's National Fraud Enforcement Division credited new fraud-detection measures implemented by the Trump administration for the arrests. He said that "this is the first international seizure of its kind in Kenya," while warning fraudsters that the crackdown has only just begun.
 
[...] At a press conference, McDonald was joined by FBI and Department of Education officials to explain how the scheme works. It starts with bad actors purchasing personally identifiable information (PII) of Americans -- most frequently targeting high school graduates who never attended college and went straight into the workforce. Once they have that sensitive data, they fill out the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) while seeking to enroll in universities and community colleges. If accepted, student aid is distributed first to schools to cover tuition and fees, but any leftover money is deposited into bank accounts controlled by the fraudsters. Dozens of Americans have opened bank accounts to act as money mules for fraudsters, the DOJ said.
 
To keep money flowing, bad actors use AI to fill out applications, complete coursework, and even make it appear that a student is attending virtual sessions. "It looks like the ghost student is actually completing the class," McDonald said at the press conference. "Some even create the appearance of a fake student in an online classroom to trick schools into believing a real person is present. The goal is to keep the ghost student in school for as long as possible, semester after semester after semester." So far, the DOE has "identified over 830,000 potentially fraudulent federal student aid accounts created by using this PII of US citizens," officials said at the press conference. If all those accounts are ghost students, total losses come close to $130 million, the DOJ said.

I remember even working through the content of a Computer Science Degree online (which is totally unnecessary if you want to learn to code,by the way).If you take a closer look, in some ways... my background may seem to disqualify me about making statements on the ease of coding. However, I can say without a single doubt, that subjects like Accounting, Physics, Engineering and even Law are more difficult than programming.Most math you learn in high-school is more difficult too, believe it; although you usually get wayyyyy more practice with algebra than writing code, which leads to a misperception as to which is more difficult.Why Coding Feels HardLearning to code is hard for a couple reasons:Installing new languages can be super frustrating. This is the first activity for a wanna-be programmer. This can create the misperception that programming is really hard because newbies extrapolate the difficulty of getting set up to how it weill be every moment after.Also, there are waayyyyyyyy too many languages, frameworks tools, libraries and plug-ins. Starting programming is super overwhelming because there are a stadezillion things to learn and you have no idea where to start.The first moments of programming are the hardest. Getting set up is annoyingly difficult and often requires learning a new way of working with computers even before you write a single line of code.Consider the instructions for installing most languages:“Open the terminal or command prompt. Type in a case-sensitive exact set of instructions to download and install the language. Use GitHub. Homebrew. Versions matter too. Are you running 32 or 64 bit? ‘Cause if you’re not sure it will crash with a cryptic error message and you’ll feel like an idiot.”These tools are learnable, like everything else, but they reinforce the impression given by the media that coding is mostly using elite tools with weird, unfriendly user interfaces. When people see coding they imagine parsing the green-streaming letters on computer screens like the movie, The Matrix; whereas the truth is a lot more like following a recipe along step-by-step.How Do You Get Over the Initial Difficulties?There’s a few ways you can do this. My favorite is to just go to the language or technology official documentation, that will tell you exactly how to set up step-by-step.Alternatively, you can dive into internet tutorials (why do you think platforms like YouTube, Quora exists?), but recognize that sometimes they are aimed at already-proficient programmers, who know what OOP and GitHub are, and are fluent with writing commands into Terminal.If you get one of these, you can try to follow it, but don’t feel bad if you screw it up. It’s frustrating and it doesn’t mean all coding will be like this.Another option is to avoid setup at all. Just use some coding tutorial website that teach you to code without needing any installation. I like this too, but sometimes you can’t actually build the thing you want to build with these apps. However, if you hate the setup, that’s where I’d start.Most important, however, is to remember that I told you this. When you try to learn to code, it will be frustrating to get set up, and just accept that this is a small price to pay. Soon it will be easier and you’ll do stuff that is cool. Don’t feel dumb because you get stuck here, I still do and I’ve been writing code for years.What Language/Framework/Library Should I Start With?This seems like a good question to ask, but, I’d argue, it’s actually the wrong way to think about learning programming.First, despite the fact that programmers often boast about how many languages they know, recognize that most languages are only superficially different. Yes, I know all about language design, so don’t tell me about the importance of scripting versus compiling, or whether a language is strongly or weakly typed. Those things matter, but they’re details.The basics of nearly all languages and tools are the same. Variables. Loops. Functions. Pointers. Data Types. OOP. Modules. These concepts exist in almost all programming languages. If you pick a mainstream language, you’ll learn these in mostly the same way, so it doesn’t matter if you pick Python, JavaScript, C++, Java or even PHP.The place languages do matter is what you want to use them for.Want to write iPhone apps? Swift or Objective C are the languages of choice. Need to create web pages? JavaScript is going to come in handy. Yes, you can use almost any language for any task if you tinker with it and get the right plug-ins. However, some languages are easier to get started with certain types of projects than others.Therefore, the first question to ask is not: which language should I learn, but, which project should I start with?What Should Be Your First Project?I recommend starting your programming adventure, even before you write a single line of code, with a decision about a concrete programming project you’d like to create.This serves a couple purposes:It narrows down the language/framework choices considerably. Once you know you’re building a website, you’re already leaning towards tools that were designed with that goal in mind.Everything you learn is connected to a destination. Transfer of learning is notoriously difficult. Learning directly by building, works better than learning something and just hoping it will help you later.You can work on something you think is cool. If you think it would be cool to make an interactive website, do that. If you’d prefer a game, do that. If you’d prefer to automate some tedious work, do that instead. Do what you feel is cool and you’ll be motivated to stick to it.In general, smaller is better when it comes to projects. Deciding to start with making the next Google is ambitious, but probably will get you stuck in the weeds before you make much progress.If your true ambitious are huge, it’s often best to work on a toy project first. Many experienced programmers still do this when they are entering a new territory of programming. Toy projects take the essential ideas of programming, but turn it into something you can do in a few days or weeks, instead of years.Examples of good projects include:A basic terminal text-adventure game. No graphics, but still requires learning concepts like loops, variables, input-output processing.A simple website. Start with just displaying a static page. Maybe add in comments, users, photos or interactive elements as you learn more.A simple app. What’s something dead-simple you’d like to have on your phone? It can be stupid to start, don’t worry.A script for automating a tedious task.In general, programs are easier when they involve no multimedia content (websites are a bit of an exception), so if you’re making a game, for instance, a text game tends to be easier than one with graphics, if only because making all the graphics can take time.Similarly, different core activities have different difficulties. Arithmetic and simple calculations done repeatedly are easiest. Processing text for exact patterns is a bit harder. Processing text for vague patterns is harder still. Processing, speech, photos and video is even harder.If you do end up picking an initial project that turns out to be super difficult, it’s okay to scale back. “Make an application that calculates my mortgage payments” is much, much easier than “Make an application that can tell you what someone’s hairstyle is from a photo.” It’s often not obvious that this is the case in the beginning, so don’t worry if you accidentally pick a “hard” problem to start with, you can adjust it later to something easier.Which Resources Should You Use?Once you’ve picked a project, the next step is to get some resources to help. This is a step many people worry over endlessly, but like the language choice, it’s a lot less important (and depends more on your goals) than you think.I won’t list specific resources, because there are so many good ones that my suggestions are going to leave out some of the best. Instead, here’s three strategies for finding good resources:Get a book that teaches you the language + project you want. There should be a computer section in your city’s bookstore or library, you can just pick any of those. I personally like O’Reilly (they publish the best software development books), but there are lots of good ones. (If you haven’t figured out which language yet, just DuckDuckGo your type of project and look for suggestions.) I read the Self-taught programmer by Cory Altoff, the first time I wanted to learn Python.Attend a MOOC. Coursera, edX, MIT, Harvard, FreeCodeCamp and others all teach computer programming online. Once again, the thing that matters most isn’t the exact class, but whether it teaches the language/project domain you care about.Stressing over which book or course to pick is the wrong thing to worry about. The main thing to do is to use the book or course to learn enough to start tinkering on your project, not to master programming on its own. Starting your project before your ready is definitely the way you should feel about it.Do What Real Programmers Do and Ask DuckDuckGo/StackOverflow/GoogleOnce you actually get started writing code, you’re going to encounter many, many situations where you either don’t know how to do something, or you learned how to do it before and you’ve forgotten.In these situations, you should do what real programmers do: ask DuckDuckGo/Google/StackOverflow. This isn’t a shameful activity, but a part of real programming. I’ve been coding for years, but I always forget silly syntactical things and so I find myself duckduckgoing regular expressions over and over again. It’s not bad, it’s just part of the process.Once you’ve gotten yourself installed, you’ve learned a bit with your book to know the basics and have started working on your first project, you’ll learn the rest by googling and adding to your library of programming knowledge. Computer science theories, detailed understandings of the language you’re working with or advanced design patterns can wait until you’ve finished a few real projects and feel like you can code something.Notice #1: Don’t Copy-and-PasteA first piece of advice when it comes to this step is to never copy-and-paste. Copy-and-pasting is bad because you don’t try to understand the code you’re copying. If you have to transcribe, in contrast, you naturally ask yourself, “why this? why not something else?” Even if you don’t have a great answer immediately, typing things for yourself will open your mind up to the answer whereas copy-and-pasting shuts down thinking.Notice #2: Try it Yourself Before Looking for a SolutionA second piece of advice is to always try to solve something yourself before looking up how someone else does it. Most problems have many, many ways they can be solved. The challenge is that expert programmers often know a particularly concise, clever way, but that often isn’t the “obvious” way.This can lead to a trap where you see a clever solution that employs tricky syntax, think that there was no way you would have guessed that solution, and believe you couldn’t have solved it on your own. That’s usually not true, yet it’s an unfortunate side effect of looking up solutions before trying to find your own.Summary of AdvThisisting up is frustrating.

items.title: The Night He Came Home
items.author: Renan Botasse
items.content:
My name is Renan. I lived in Colatina, Brazil.

When I was a kid, Halloween did not exist on my street. October arrived hot, with the smell of the Rio Doce in the air and the late afternoon taking its time to go dark. There was no candy at the door, no costumes lined up on the sidewalk. There was, instead, the house we crossed faster, the one someone swore had a story. There were the adults’ warnings: don’t talk to strangers; don’t take long coming back; say where you are. Above all, there was the idea that something could cross the short distance between the gate and the corner and never return a child.

In Colatina, “witch” was not a costume imported from an American calendar. It was a word that dropped the volume of a conversation. I still did not know what that meant for real. I only knew that terror did not need a mask to work.

Years later, in a dark room, small TV, volume low so the house would not wake up, I reached , John Carpenter’s 1978 film, for the first time. I don’t remember if it was October. I remember the silence after the final credit. I remember thinking that film, shot in a suburb I had never seen, spoke to a fear I already knew: the quiet street, the half-open door, the “why” that never comes. It felt closer to real dread than any story where the monster explains the monster.

Maybe no one can fully explain what makes so effective. The most we can do, today, is try to understand a few facts.

In cinema, Halloween always existed. In American life, too: candy, costumes, the “haunted house” down the street. In Carpenter’s film, the date is not decoration. It is the thesis.

The story begins in 1963, on a Halloween night in Haddonfield. A six-year-old boy kills his own sister. Fifteen years later, in 1978, he escapes a psychiatric institution and returns to town. The film does not invent the slasher, but it organizes the genre with an almost cruel clarity: quiet suburb, teenage girl alone, heavy breathing offscreen, and a man, or what is left of a man, reduced to a silhouette.

Carpenter and Debra Hill wrote the screenplay in about ten days. The producers had come to him with the idea of a killer who hunted babysitters. There were rumors the original title would be ; Yablans, one of the producers, denied it. The film was always going to take place on Halloween. Carpenter liked that. It seemed too obvious, and for that very reason, no one had fully embraced the date until then.

Haddonfield, Illinois, is fiction. The name came from Debra Hill’s hometown in New Jersey. The county on the police badge points to Bowling Green, where Carpenter grew up. Laurie Strode carries the name of an old girlfriend of the director. Michael Myers, that of a British producer. Tommy Doyle and Dr. Samuel Loomis are Hitchcock echoes: and . Jamie Lee Curtis, in her first film, was the daughter of Janet Leigh. American cinema loves those invisible threads. Carpenter did too.

The budget was small, somewhere around $325,000. Donald Pleasence, as Loomis, made $20,000. Jamie Lee Curtis, $8,000. Nick Castle, under the mask, $25 a day. The mask came from a costume shop: a William Shatner face, Captain Kirk, bought for less than two dollars, painted white, the eyes widened. The actors’ own clothes, cars rented from a local dealer, dead leaves reused from scene to scene. Shot in spring, in California, with palm trees hidden in the frame and license plates kept out of the way to fake the Midwest. Robert Englund, years before Freddy Krueger, helped scatter leaves to manufacture autumn.

The film made tens of millions. But the number matters less than the feeling it left behind: that evil could live in the empty house at the end of the street, the one every child knows, even without knowing the name of whoever died inside.

In real life, after an atrocity, the first question is usually the same: why?

The human brain does not tolerate emptiness well. It wants motive, biography, trauma, a bank account, revenge. It wants to turn the absurd into an algorithm. refuses that comfort.

Michael Myers, in the credits, appears as . He is not a character in the classic sense. He is a presence. Loomis insists on calling him “it,” not “he.” Evil. A force. Something you watch, fear, try to lock away, and that still crosses the night.

There are readings. Michael saw sex too young and could not understand it. Laurie would remind him of Judith, the sister. Tommy, beside her when she drops the key at the Myers house, would be about the age Michael was in 1963. The killings would follow a ritual pattern: bedsheets, an improvised shrine, a body arranged like a scene. All of that may be true. None of it is stated in the 1978 film with the authority of a caption.

That is where the film parts ways with so many of its successors. has territory and revenge. A Nightmare on Elm Street has collective guilt. Michael, in the first film, has absence. The mask does not only hide the face: it hides intent. Without expression, we do not know if he enjoys it, if he hates, if he feels nothing at all. Without a “why,” the “what” gets worse.

The sequels tried to fill the hole: siblings, curses, supernatural answers. Some of those solutions land. None, to my mind, beats the question left open. Explaining Michael is domesticating him. And domestic fear, the residential street, the half-open door, loses its force when it becomes a manual.

Carpenter and Hill also said later that Laurie’s survival was not a prize for virginity, a Freudian reading critics fastened on too quickly. Laurie survives because she pays attention. Because she is not distracted. Because, in the end, she fights back. The rest is couch theory.

How you film what has no name

The film opens with a long shot, almost voyeuristic, through the killer’s eyes. The inspiration points back to Orson Welles’s : a take that forces us to follow the crime as accomplices. At the end, the mask comes off and we see a child. The shock is not only the murder. It is the age.

The score, by Carpenter himself, in time signatures his father taught him, does half the work. The story goes that an executive watched the film without the music and did not find it scary. With the score, he changed his mind. A few notes. Enough.

Dean Cundey, the cinematographer, and the early use of the Panaglide give the film that restless glide: the camera follows, breathes, does not cut to spare us. The spaces keep getting smaller: street, house, room, closet. At the start, there is a world. By the end, there is creaking wood and almost nowhere left to run.

There is also the dry humor of cheap production turning into style. Precarious lighting that swallows detail. The asylum car appearing in the background while Laurie talks. Myers driving with the mask dead straight, an image at once terrifying and absurd. Annie in the laundry room, and us, who saw what she did not, begging in our heads: don’t go that way.

The safe suburb, the cliché the film helped crystallize, works because Carpenter films observation first, not the slaughter. Michael is a stalker before he is an executioner. The paranoia builds in the corner of the frame. When the violence arrives, it is already late: the fear came first.

Samhain, the haunted house, and what remains

Behind the scenes, people talk about Samhain, the Celtic festival when the dead cross the veil. They talk about evil that cannot be killed. They talk about the Myers house as the haunted house every town invents for itself. Carpenter wanted that universal recognition: the place you walk past faster, without admitting why.

Loomis describes Michael with the coldness of someone who spent fifteen years staring into an abyss that stared back. Pleasence took the role after Cushing and Christopher Lee turned it down. Lee would later call that refusal the biggest mistake of his career. In a few days of shooting, a friendship with Carpenter was born that would lead to other films.

In the end, Loomis shoots. Six times. In the heart. Michael falls. Then he is gone. The film does not celebrate victory. It offers a montage of empty places, the house, the street, the night, with the breathing still on top. He could be anywhere. Including, the cut suggests, nowhere.

It is an honest ending. Because the fear stages is not the fear of a monster with clear rules. It is the fear of explanatory emptiness. The same emptiness that makes a small inland town invent witches when it cannot stand being without a cause. The same one that makes an adult, decades later, remember a street in Colatina at dusk and feel the stomach close, not because of a movie ghost, but because of the old certainty that the dark, there, never needed subtitles.

A note, if a note belongs

I am not saying a 1978 horror film and the fear of growing up in a small town are the same thing. They are not. One is an artifact. The other is memory. But both, each in its way, deal with the same human difficulty: what to do when the “why” does not come.

runs a little over ninety minutes and costs almost nothing on paper. It still scares because it respects the viewer’s intelligence, and because it respects the terror of not knowing. Simplicity. Ambiguity. One night. One street. A white shape walking without hurry.

Halloween, on the calendar, is make-believe. In Carpenter’s film, it is a warning.

This is the night he came home.

And the question that remains, the only one the film refuses to kill along with the victims, is not whether Michael Myers is a man, a demon, or a cheap-production accident.

It is another, older, and far less comfortable:

If evil needs no reason to cross your street… anyone can be its victim, without warning, without sense, again, without motive.

U.S. technology stocks plunged for a second consecutive day on Friday as investors grew increasingly concerned about the enormous cost of artificial intelligence development and whether those investments will pay off. The Nasdaq fell more than 3.5%, while Intel shares dropped as much as 30%, Reddit fell 26%, and Alphabet extended its losses after shedding more than $500 billion in market value Thursday. The BBC notes that Meta, Alphabet, Oracle, Amazon, and Microsoft have collectively committed to spending $800.6 billion on AI in 2026. From the report: Chris Low, from investment management firm FHN Financial, said the bulk of what was happening in the stock market was in reaction to some of the biggest tech players such as Amazon and Google. He told Reuters the companies were "showing some pretty significant growing pains as they aggressively pursue the AI build-out." "The thinking is that these signs suggest that the entire sector is going to slow down."
 
Kathleen Brookes, research director at trading firm XTB, said there have been many ups and downs in AI trade in recent months. "Investors have turned ruthless, punishing any signs of disappointment in [third quarter] earnings," she said. "The AI trade has had a good run in recent years, but now investors want payback, and companies like Alphabet and Intel are in the crosshairs." [...] Brookes noted that November is typically a strong month for stocks. "If we see AI stocks continue to struggle in the coming days, it could suggest the AI trade is past its peak, and investors will be looking for a new theme to drive markets," she said.

items.title: GM Reaches $220 Million Settlement Over Selling Drivers' Private Data
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from TechCrunch: General Motors will pay $220 million to 36 states to settle allegations that it illegally sold private driving behavior and location information to data brokers. As part of the settlement, GM must get drivers' express consent before it collects or shares their driving and location data -- terms that are in line with separate agreements it previously reached with California and the Federal Trade Commission (FTC). This settlement does contain a new requirement that GM must have a third party assess the automaker's compliance with the privacy program it has put in place.
 
The agreement announced Thursday settles a lawsuit brought by a coalition of attorneys general from 36 states that alleged GM had sold the information to data brokers, which in turn then sold it to insurance providers. "This agreement addresses Smart Driver, a product we ended in 2024, and reinforces steps we've taken to strengthen our privacy practices," GM said in an emailed statement. "Safer, more helpful and personalized experiences are enabled by connected vehicle data, and GM is committed to being clear about what information is used, how it's protected, and the choices customers have about what they share."
 
The settlement comes more than two years after a New York Times report showed how GM and OnStar collected, used, and sold drivers' precise geolocation data and driving behavior to third parties, including data brokers LexisNexis and Verisk. The data was collected through GM's Smart Driver program, a free feature contained within its connected car apps that tracked and rated driving behaviors and seat belt use. Data brokers sold this information to insurance providers, which could affect customers' rates, the NYT reported at the time.

items.title: UK Social Media Ban May Lock Out More Than 100,000 Teens Without ID
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Under the UK's planned social media ban, more than 100,000 British teenagers aged 16 and 17 could initially be locked out of social media because they lack a passport or driving license that may be needed as a fallback for age verification. The Guardian reports: Ofcom, the UK's online watchdog, said about 150,000 16- to 17-year-olds do not own a passport or driving licence, which are likely to be needed to access age-restricted platforms. The Australia-style ban on under-16s accessing social media services, including Instagram, TikTok and YouTube, is due to come into force next spring. The head of Ofcom, Melanie Dawes, said "motivated children" would seek to bypass the restrictions, as has happened in Australia.
 
On Thursday, Ofcom published an assessment of age verification measures that could underpin the ban, outlining four "highly effective" methods: checking a person's official ID against a live selfie, a bank verifying an account holder's age, an official digital ID service like the Young Scot card, or estimating someone's age via a selfie. However, the watchdog said a form of official ID would probably be needed as a "backstop" for other methods, such as facial age estimation, which could be inaccurate by several years. Ofcom said a cohort of 16- to 17-year-olds could miss out as a result. "This means that people without a form of photo ID will likely need to take steps to obtain one to access age-restricted services," the regulator said. The report notes that more than nine out of 10 Britons over 16 have passports or driving licenses.
 
"We should expect that motivated children will seek to bypass the restrictions -- just like alcohol laws can't completely eradicate underage drinking -- but there'll be ways for platforms to mitigate this risk," said Dawes. "This will be a huge cultural shift for our society, so it'll take time to adjust, and everyone will have a part to play."

items.title: Reddit Will Force Everyone to Log In
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Reddit plans to require users to log in to browse the platform, ending its longstanding practice of allowing anonymous visitors to access posts and discussions. According to CEO Steve Huffman, a key reason behind the decision is to curb unauthorized scraping and automated traffic.
 
"This is a big change for Reddit, where we've allowed logged-out access to basically all of Reddit for the last two decades," Huffman says. "And I don't know about you, but as someone whose life has been defined by the open internet, it's a big change for me. But I've come to the conclusion that this is the right decision for our platform and the right decision for our business." The Verge reports: There's no definitive timeline on when this change will roll out to all users, or how the site will work if you're logged out. (If I send my friend a link to a thread and they aren't logged in, what will they see?) To start, Reddit will test the logged-in requirement in "select markets outside the US" in the "coming months," according to CEO Steve Huffman. "We'll look at the impact on the user experience, on our business, and on the whole Reddit ecosystem, figure out where the right boundaries are, and go from there." Reddit has also rebuilt and is rereleasing the Reddit app's incognito mode.
 
Huffman claims the login requirement is better for Reddit's user experience and its ads business and is "more protective of Reddit data." The "vast majority" of unauthorized Reddit access happens "through our logged-out experiences," though the company will still strike licensing deals of its data with companies, like the deals it made with OpenAI and Google in 2024. Huffman notes that Reddit does not need to know a logged-in user's identity -- "Honestly, we don't want to know" -- just that the user is logged in at all. And he says that more logged-in users lets the company deliver "more relevant ads."

items.title: Binance Suffers Biggest Crypto Hack In History With $6.3 Billion Affected [UPDATE]
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
UPDATE 10/30/26: Binance has temporarily suspended customer withdrawals after suffering what investigators say is the biggest crypto hack in history. According to Binance CEO Yi He, the company estimates roughly $6.3 billion in funds were impacted, with roughly $3 billion in assets frozen on-chain so far. Rest assured, "your money is safe, and we're covering every loss," said co-CEO Richard Teng in a LinkedIn post.
 
"This was a complex attack," said Teng. "The attacker also used a self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and tracers, making it more difficult for us to trace." From a report: Teng said the incident was not carried out by one person. While the initial investigation indicated the involvement of a compromised laptop, further digging revealed additional points of breach. [...] Blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Elliptic have linked the theft to North Korean hackers, with TRM attributing it "with high confidence" to a group known as TraderTraitor, the same group responsible for last year's Bybit hack.
 
Elliptic estimated Friday that about 44% of the stolen assets have been frozen, with stablecoins accounting for nearly all of those funds. The firm estimated that attackers still controlled over $3 billion in crypto that token issuers cannot directly freeze.
 
The hackers appear to have compromised Binance's wallet-signing infrastructure, allowing them to authorize transactions that drained billions of dollars in cryptocurrency across multiple blockchains, according to the firms. Binance, in its preliminary stage, has conducted an investigation into the hack, which suggests the incident may have begun with a compromised engineer's laptop. The exchange added that it has found no evidence that wallet passwords were leaked. Below is the original story from yesterday, Oct. 29th. 
Binance is investigating a potential hack after more than $2 billion in crypto was drained from one of its wallets into a new external account, with Blockaid estimating nearly $3.3 billion was moved.
 
"Our teams are aware of reports of a potential security issue and are actively investigating," said Binance on X.
 
"User funds are safe," said Binance founder CZ. "It does look like a hack on Binance. Appreciate the quick freeze from Tether (~$971m) and Circle (~$823m). I don't manage Binance anymore, but as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered."
 
At around the same time, crypto-based prediction market Polymarket reported its own security incident that wiped out around $2.7 million in user funds.

items.title: The Tragedy of Losing Your Wikipedia Page
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes an excerpt from a Wired article that explores the often-contentious process of nominating pages for deletion when their subjects fail to meet the encyclopedia's notability standards: What do you need to know -- need to know -- about Xavier Trudeau? The eldest son of former Canadian prime minister Justin, the teenage Trudeau has recently begun performing R&B under the mononym Xav. But, with all due respect to Xav, do those facts make him a person of note? Should you expect to be able to read about him on Wikipedia? What about Evanescence guitarist Tim McCord, or 2012 Yachtmaster of the Year Rainer Holtorff? All three have had a biography on Wikipedia; all three of those biographies were considered for deletion this year on the grounds that the subjects were not notable enough to warrant a biography at all. Every day, dozens, sometimes hundreds, of Wikipedia biographies -- of child actors turned LA realtors, retired ambassadors, soccer players who have played less than 10 minutes of professional soccer -- are purged from the world's free encyclopedia.
 
It's not as though Wikipedia, which hosts over 7 million articles in the English language, doesn't have the space. But Wikipedia has only so many volunteers to monitor its contents. To this day, Wikipedia editors are discovering hoaxes that have gone undetected for decades. The time it takes to verify the release dates of Xav's three singles is better spent -- the logic goes -- by asking whether the American Civil War officer Nathaniel Lyon really drank mustard during battle, as was claimed in his Wikipedia biography for 17 years. Wikipedia removed the mustard claim, not because it was proven wrong, but because there was no reliable evidence for it. "We're not really looking for what's true," Britta Gustafson, who has been editing Wikipedia since 2001, told me. "We're looking for what's verifiable." Wikipedia editors do not themselves decide that a person is not notable, only that there is a lack of reliable evidence to support the claim...

By @marshyon [ 6 Min read ] AI promises greater productivity, but dependence comes at a cost. Read More.

By @zbruceli [ 15 Min read ] Didn't wait for Meta's Muse Charm. Built my own AI pal on a $21 ESP32 stick. Read More.

items.author: sarahevans
items.content:
: A KDD 2026 paper follows five customer support AI agents through testing and deployment. The team checks automated graders against expert judgments, starts new versions at 1% to 5% exposure, and tracks whether satisfaction gains come with more self-service or more work for human agents.

An automated grader can give an AI agent a passing score and still be wrong. In, engineers at a digital bank report that one grader initially performed worse than simply choosing the most common answer. Before relying on it to evaluate customer-facing agents, they had to improve the evaluator itself.

The paper describes how a bank serving more than 100 million users tests agentic AI in production across card delivery, debt management, credit limits, card management and product explanation. That customer base provides context for the deployment; it is not the test sample size.

For companies buying agentic AI, the case offers a view into how a team decides an agent is ready to handle more work. The evidence comes from customer support, rather than paid media or back-office workflows. Its useful contribution is the detail behind each readiness decision, from the tests a new version must pass to the point where a person takes over.

All Five AI Agents Improved Satisfaction but Scored Below Human Benchmarks

All five agents improved transactional Net Promoter Score (tNPS), collected after a support interaction, in online A/B tests. The comparison varied by agent, including earlier versions and a control group. Scores nevertheless remained below the bank’s expert human-agent benchmarks, which were measured separately within the support funnel.

Compared with human agents

Source: Gupta et al., KDD 2026, Table 3. Human scores were measured separately from the AI scores.

The self-service rate tracks how many requests the AI resolved without handing them to a person. Card delivery posted the largest gain, 29 percentage points, alongside a 37-point rise in satisfaction. The product explainer was the one exception, with a slight dip the authors attribute to temporary errors in calls to the language model.

The Automated Grader Initially Scored Below a Simple Baseline

The team separates an agent’s instructions and business procedures into modules that can be revised individually. Domain experts change those modules, then language models acting as automated graders evaluate candidate versions before live testing.

To establish the reference answers, three operations analysts labeled each evaluation sample and explained their decisions. Majority vote determined the final label. Those explanations then helped GEPA, a prompt-optimization method, refine the graders’ instructions.

On customer input verification, the initial grader scored 68.88% accuracy. Always choosing the most common label would have scored 77.78%. Optimization raised accuracy to 88.89%, measuring agreement with the expert labels rather than the customer-facing agent’s overall accuracy.

The authors also tested whether different grader models agreed after optimization. Those tests covered models from one vendor, leaving broader model coverage for future work.

New Agent Versions Start With 1% to 5% Exposure

Offline checks let the team test targeted fixes before exposing customers to them. Live metrics then reveal problems those checks missed, including changes in escalation patterns. New versions begin at 1% to 5% exposure while the team tracks self-service, tNPS, escalations and errors.

The bank’s agents transfer conversations to people when a request falls outside their routines, necessary data cannot be retrieved or confidence is low. According to the authors, the agents operate within existing policies and human oversight, without unrestricted or irreversible decisions about credit or debt management.

Some handoffs can be removed by giving an agent the tools to finish a defined task. In the card-delivery deployment, adding a card-reissue capability removed the need for a human transfer from the most common resolution path. Other handoffs remain part of the operating design.

Average handle time can rise even when automation is working. If AI resolves simpler requests, the human team is left with harder cases that take longer.

“AI should take the parts of a customer interaction that slow an agent down, so the agent can spend their judgment where it counts,” said Erin Walker, Global Vice President of CX AI, Business & Delivery at TELUS Digital.

The company’s framework for also covers adoption and change management. Any routing change lands on the team receiving the transferred cases, and that team needs the customer’s context and the capacity to take them on.

A higher satisfaction score can come from sending more difficult cases to people and leaving simpler requests with the AI. Evaluating agentic AI in production therefore means examining why cases escalated. A missing tool and a decision reserved for human judgment call for different responses. The satisfaction score alone cannot show whether the agent improved or the workload moved.

items.title: First Wired XR Glasses Powered By Android XR
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
XREAL has launched the AURA, its first wired augmented reality glasses powered by Google's Android XR platform. They feature transparent Micro-OLED displays, a 70-degree field of view, Gemini AI integration, and a Snapdragon Reality Elite processor. TechPowerUp reports: The device is built around a simple idea: your apps, screens, entertainment, and AI assistant should be able to come with you wherever you go. On day-one, users have access to millions of familiar mobile apps and games from Google Play, alongside many experiences specifically for XR. Android XR brings familiar hand and voice inputs to AURA, while Gemini makes the experiences more natural and intuitive by working across what users see and do.
 
With Wired Mirroring, users can plug a computer or handheld gaming console directly into XREAL AURA via USB-C and instantly turn it into a massive private spatial window. That means a laptop, handheld gaming device, or other compatible USB-C device can sit alongside native Android XR apps in a user's spatial workspace. Whether turning a plane seat into a private multi-monitor setup, watching a movie on a large virtual screen, or playing Android and console games in an immersive spatial environment, XREAL AURA is designed to make spatial computing practical, portable, and useful.
 
[...] For work, AURA creates a portable multi-window workspace without requiring a physical monitor. Users can open Android XR apps, mirror a laptop, place windows in virtual space, and use Gemini to help understand or act on what is on screen. For entertainment, AURA becomes a private theater on demand. Users can access familiar streaming apps, expand content into a large virtual display, and use electrochromic dimming to create a more immersive viewing experience while remaining aware of their surroundings when needed. For play, AURA supports Android games and compatible mirrored gaming devices, enabling users to play on a large and immersive private display. The glasses are available to order today, with limited-time pricing starting at $1,099 for the 12GB RAM and 256GB storage model. Devices are expected to begin shipping in mid-November.

items.title: Fed Holds Rates at 3.75%–4.00% in a 10–2 Vote: How QQQ, SPY and Bitcoin Reacted
items.author: Testing MEXC
items.content:
Two officials, Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, dissented in favor of another quarter-point increase.

Markets now see a December hike as likely: CME FedWatch priced an 85.0% chance after the close, up from 78.3% a day earlier, Reuters reported.

The S&P 500 rose 0.28% and the Nasdaq Composite 0.27%, and on MEXC the bigger moves in QQQ and SPY contracts came after the closing bell, when Microsoft and Alphabet reported.

●      The FOMC held the federal funds rate at 3.75%–4.00% by a 10–2 vote, with Cook and Hammack preferring a 25-basis-point hike.

●      Growth was upgraded to a “strong pace,” and the Fed said it will wait for more information before deciding its next move.

●      Chair Kevin Warsh did not commit to a hike, but futures moved toward one, with odds rising to 85.0%.

●      Warsh said one 2027 meeting will become a strategy session with no rate decision, leaving seven rate-setting meetings.

●      Stocks closed slightly higher, the two-year Treasury yield slipped to 4.722% and the dollar index fell 0.2%.

●      From 1:55 p.m. ET to the 4:00 p.m. close, QQQUSDT rose 0.38%, SPYUSDT 0.08% and BTCUSDT 0.89%; after the bell, QQQUSDT gave back 0.74% as Alphabet fell.

What Did the Fed Decide in October 2026?

The Fed left the target range for the federal funds rate at 3-3/4 to 4 percent, according to the FOMC statement.

The interest rate on reserve balances stays at 3.90%.

Cook and Hammack voted against the decision because they preferred to raise rates by a quarter point; Reuters noted it was Cook’s first policy dissent.

The September 16 meeting had raised rates by a quarter point on a 12–0 vote.

What Changed in the Fed Statement?

The October statement is close to September’s, with three edits that matter.

●      economic activity is now described as expanding at a “strong pace,” up from “solid.”

●      the sentence saying the September hike would support a timelier return to the 2% goal.

●      a line saying the accumulation of more information will help the Committee decide the appropriate policy stance.

The Committee kept its line that inflation remains elevated and that it “will deliver price stability.”

It also kept describing productivity growth as strong and capital investment as robust, the same AI-era investment that Microsoft and Alphabet reported on a few hours later.

What Did Warsh Say About a December Rate Hike?

Warsh did not commit to a December move. He said the coming weeks would bring a lot of data that leaves the Committee better placed to decide, according to Reuters.

That calendar is crowded: the Q3 GDP report on October 29, the midterm elections on November 3, October payrolls on November 6 and October CPI on November 10.

September CPI, the last reading before the meeting, showed inflation at 3.7% from a year earlier, with core at 2.6%.

Warsh said politics played no role in the decision, and that he did not think the economy was too hot, although most colleagues disagreed with him.

He argued inflation can return to 2% without slower growth or job losses, and that higher rates are already tightening credit, Reuters reported.

Why Is the Fed Changing Its Meeting Schedule?

Warsh said the Fed will keep eight meetings a year, but some will focus on long-term strategy without a rate vote, Reuters reported.

●      one strategy meeting and seven rate-setting meetings.

●      two strategy meetings and six rate-setting meetings.

He did not say which meetings will change, and the Fed has not yet published a formal release; its 2027 calendar still lists eight regular meetings.

For traders, fewer rate-setting meetings mean fewer scheduled rate-decision days, and more weight on each one that remains.

How Did Markets React to the Fed Hold?

Wall Street ended slightly higher.

●      up 0.28% to 7,743.97.

●      up 0.27% to 26,549.85.

●      up 0.19% to 52,475.10.

The two-year Treasury yield slipped 1.46 basis points to 4.722%, while longer-dated yields rose and the yield curve steepened after the press conference.

The dollar index fell 0.2% to 102.15, according to Reuters.

Oil stayed in focus: Brent settled 1% higher at $115.32 and US crude 3% higher at $102.78 after an attack on a Saudi refinery, keeping energy at the center of the inflation debate.

How QQQ, SPY and BTC Perpetuals Reacted on MEXC

Our Fed rate decision preview set four checkpoints for the night: the 2:00 p.m. statement, the 2:30 p.m. press conference, the 4:00 p.m. close and the 00:00 UTC funding settlement.

QQQUSDT, SPYUSDT and BTCUSDT 5-minute closes, indexed to 1:55 p.m. ET on October 28, 2026. Source: MEXC public futures API.

the first reaction was small. Between the statement and the press conference, QQQUSDT dipped as much as 0.24% from 723.73 USDT and was back at 723.64 by 2:30 p.m. SPYUSDT was 0.08% lower and BTCUSDT 0.09% higher.

2:30 p.m. press conference: activity picked up as Warsh spoke. The 2:30 p.m. five-minute bar in QQQUSDT traded about 1.31 million USDT, ten times the hour before it. By the 4:00 p.m. close, QQQUSDT was up 0.38% from 1:55 p.m., SPYUSDT 0.08% and BTCUSDT 0.89%, at 81,544.7 USDT.

the larger move came from earnings. QQQUSDT jumped to 728.11 in the first five minutes after the bell as Microsoft rose, then fell to 721.05 by 5:00 p.m. as Alphabet dropped about 10%, a 0.74% slide from the close. SPYUSDT fell 0.29% over the same hour and BTCUSDT 0.31%.

QQQUSDT and SPYUSDT both settled at 0% at 00:00 UTC on October 29, unchanged from the previous settlement. Positive funding would have been a cost to longs; the derivatives market added no extra pressure either way.

On a Fed night, QQQ moved more after the close than in the two hours after the statement, which shows how much of the index now rides on a handful of megacap reports.

Following QQQ and SPY Through MEXC

For eligible users considering share ownership, MEXC RealStocks is a separate route; check availability and supported securities directly.

Perpetual contracts do not confer shareholder rights and carry funding, leverage and liquidation risks.

Did the Fed raise rates in October 2026?

No. The FOMC held the federal funds rate at 3.75%–4.00% on October 28, 2026, by a 10–2 vote. Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack preferred a quarter-point hike.

Will the Fed raise rates in December 2026?

It is not decided. Warsh did not commit to a move, but CME FedWatch priced an 85.0% chance of a 25-basis-point hike at the December 8–9 meeting after the decision.

What changed in the October 2026 Fed statement?

The Fed upgraded growth to a “strong pace,” removed the sentence explaining its September hike, and said more information will help it decide its next move.

How did QQQ and SPY react to the Fed decision?

QQQUSDT on MEXC rose 0.38% from 1:55 p.m. ET to the 4:00 p.m. close and SPYUSDT 0.08%. In the cash market, the S&P 500 closed up 0.28% and the Nasdaq Composite up 0.27%.

How did Bitcoin react to the Fed decision?

BTCUSDT on MEXC rose 0.89% from 1:55 p.m. ET to 4:00 p.m., to 81,544.7 USDT, then gave back 0.31% in the following hour as tech earnings hit stock futures.

How many FOMC meetings will there be in 2027?

The Fed will still meet eight times, but Warsh said one 2027 meeting will be a strategy session without a rate decision, leaving seven rate-setting meetings.

What is the FOMC interest rate decision?

It is the Fed’s announcement of its target range for the federal funds rate after each FOMC meeting; our glossary explains the FOMC interest rate decision in more detail.

Discover wallets, check PnL and automatically copy buys and sells on Solana with your own trade sizes and execution limits.

Keeping up manually means catching each move, sizing your trade and getting the swap filled. Blockchain.ai automates the process from a funded trading vault using the user’s settings, with copying continuing after the browser tab closes.

Find Solana wallets and check their track record

The includes profiles such as and , alongside other Solana traders. Users can search by name or X handle, inspect associated wallets, or paste a Solana address from outside the directory.

Available wallet analytics include trade history, token holdings and 7D, 30D and 90D realized PnL, ROI and win rate. Users can research wallets before connecting their own. For traders with several wallets, copying follows only the specific address selected.

Set trade sizing, slippage and buy limits

Scaled sizing follows the share of available trading funds spent by the target wallet. Fixed sizing uses a chosen dollar amount for each new copied buy. Sells follow the proportion of the position sold by the target wallet.

Cash out requests swaps back into the asset used to fund the vault and a withdrawal to the user’s wallet. Withdraw tokens lets users withdraw remaining tokens without swapping them first. Liquidity, execution requirements and network fees apply.

items.title: Proton CEO Is In 'Full AI Psychosis'
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
According to 404 Media, Proton CEO Andy Yen is aggressively pushing AI adoption while fostering what workers describe as a culture of fear that discourages raising security concerns or challenging leadership. The investigation is based on interviews with eight current and one former Proton employees, as well as internal Slack chats, meeting recordings, and an AI manifesto written by the company's CTO. Longtime Slashdot reader devnulljapan summarizes the findings: Engineers at Proton, which makes the encrypted email service Proton Mail and a suite of privacy- and security-focused products, including an encrypted drive service, an authenticator app, and a password manager, are being pushed to "stop lovingly handcrafting all our code and use AI more." Workers describe an environment where employees have genuine concerns about security or being asked to develop security products with AI but feel unable to voice them, lest Yen berates them in front of everyone or threatens their employment at the company. "The CEO is in full AI psychosis and has been for a while now," one of the sources told 404 Media. Yen reportedly dismissed an employee's request for additional security testing before releasing new code, calling it "bullshit and loser thinking" and insisting that "only losers think like that." In a separate exchange over Proton's post-quantum encryption rollout, Yen criticized how the company communicated the feature's limitations and told employees that "perception is more important than truth, the truth doesn't matter if you don't win on perception."
 
"The train is coming, get onboard or get crushed. Don't be the professional fax machine operator in the internet age," Yen wrote to the security Slack channel. "I think by the end of this year most developers stop programming and start writing specs for tests that AI will code and run, to validate AI written code that humans will no longer be able to review. This will be the last year that we hire engineers, and starting next year we hire what we used to call product managers, to build things with AI."

items.title: AI-Assisted Reconciliation of Enterprise Data: Detecting and Explaining Cross-Platform Discrepancies
items.author: ajaysikharam
items.content:
Deterministic checks find the gaps. AI helps people understand them.

Last quarter's revenue was $14.6 million. Or $14.2 million. Or $14.1 million. The ledger says one thing. The Lakehouse table feeding your BI says another. The dashboard the board looked at this morning says a third.

None of the three numbers is obviously wrong, and that is the problem. When the same metric lives in several systems, each with its own refresh schedule, transformations and quirks, the numbers drift apart. Reconciliation is the work of finding where they disagree and deciding which one, if any, you trust. Done by hand, it is slow, it misses things, and it scales badly as you add systems.

I split the job in two. Deterministic checks establish the facts: row counts, sums, join-key coverage. AI handles triage and explanation. It learns which differences are normal, ranks the ones that are not, and drafts a plain-language account of what probably happened. The checks give you the truth. The AI makes it something a person can act on.

Start with checks that cannot lie

Before any model gets involved, you need checks that are plain arithmetic. For every metric you reconcile, run the same small battery of comparisons:

  • Sums of the measures that matter
  • Join-key coverage, so no business key silently vanishes
  • Hash comparisons on a sample of rows, to catch silent corruption

Run them on a schedule. The output is a table of differences with no interpretation. Nothing here needs AI, and that is deliberate. When an engineer asks why a dashboard changed overnight, the first answer should come from a check that can be re-run and gives the same result every time.

The trouble with deterministic checks is volume, not accuracy. On a real pipeline they fire constantly, and most of what they flag is expected:

  • Time zone cutoffs make one feed's Fridays look short.
  • Late-arriving rows land after the extract ran.
  • Currency rounding shaves fractions off totals.
  • Two teams define revenue differently, gross versus net, and nobody wrote it down.
  • A dashboard cache lags the Lakehouse by an hour.

A human reviewer has to learn all of this, and the knowledge lives in people's heads. Two reviewers disagree on what is worth chasing. Context switching eats hours, and the checks keep firing either way.

Let the model learn what normal looks like

This is where AI earns its place. Feed it the history of past reconciliations, meaning every flagged difference and how it was resolved. Two things happen:

  1.  A statistical baseline of normal variance for each check tells you that a half-percent gap the morning after a load is routine, while the same gap on a different feed is not.
  2. Explanations from history. An LLM gets the current difference plus the closest entries from the resolution log and drafts a short explanation with the evidence attached.

Differences that match a known pattern get labeled and logged instead of escalated. The rest are ranked by dollar impact, how new the pattern is, and whether it is getting worse.

Reviewers notice the next part most. Instead of a row reading TABLE_A.SALES_TOTAL != TABLE_B.SALES_TOTAL, they get a sentence saying what probably happened and why. Nobody has to decode column names before the coffee kicks in.

Go back to the three figures at the top: ledger $14.6M, lakehouse $14.2M, dashboard $14.1M. The deterministic check compares order counts and revenue per fulfillment center between the source system and the lakehouse table:

SELECT
  COALESCE(s.center, l.center)                   AS center,
  COALESCE(s.orders, 0)                          AS source_orders,
  COALESCE(l.orders, 0)                          AS lakehouse_orders,
  COALESCE(s.orders, 0) - COALESCE(l.orders, 0)  AS order_gap,
  COALESCE(s.revenue, 0) - COALESCE(l.revenue, 0) AS revenue_gap
FROM (SELECT center, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(amount) AS revenue
      FROM source.orders
      WHERE order_date >= '2026-07-01' AND order_date < '2026-10-01'
      GROUP BY center) s
FULL OUTER JOIN
     (SELECT center, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(amount) AS revenue
      FROM lakehouse.orders
      WHERE order_date >= '2026-07-01' AND order_date < '2026-10-01'
      GROUP BY center) l
  ON s.center = l.center
WHERE COALESCE(s.orders, 0) <> COALESCE(l.orders, 0)
   OR COALESCE(s.revenue, 0) <> COALESCE(l.revenue, 0);

It returns one row and says nothing about why:

The AI layer takes that row and the resolution log. The log shows OH-01 had the same gap on two earlier closes, both traced to the 2 a.m. extract.

OH-01 is missing about 12,000 orders (~$412K) in the lakehouse. The source extract ran at 2 a.m., before the late-day batch landed. This matches two earlier closes. Likely cause: extract timing, not data loss. Confidence: medium. Attached: row counts, extract timestamps, and the two prior resolutions.

A reviewer re-runs the extract, the gap closes, and the log records the cause as . That explains the $0.4M gap between the ledger and the lakehouse. The dashboard's remaining $0.1M is cache lag, a known pattern, so the model labels it and logs it without escalating.

This is the order that works:

  1. Name the reconciliation points. For every metric that matters, write down the source system, the lakehouse table and the report. If you cannot name all three, start there.
  2. Write the deterministic checks first. Row counts, sums, join-key coverage and hash sampling. Run them on every load, not once a month.
  3. Keep a structured resolution log. Every flagged difference gets a row: what it was, its cause category, how it resolved and who closed it. This log is the training data for everything that follows.
  4.  Variance baselines, prioritization and plain-language explanations.
  5. Keep people on the exceptions. Route anything the model cannot explain confidently to a reviewer, with the raw numbers attached. The model drafts and a person signs off.

Tradeoffs and where it goes wrong

  • Explanations can sound confident and be wrong: A model can invent a plausible cause for a difference it does not understand. Treat every explanation as a draft attached to evidence and keep the raw check data one click away.
  • The model learns your mistakes. If reviewers wrongly closed a real break as normal, the model will suppress it next time. Spot-check a sample of auto-labeled "normal" differences on a regular schedule.
  • The log is only as good as the discipline behind it. If reviewers close differences with notes like "looked fine", the model learns nothing. Use cause categories instead of free text.
  •  The AI layer adds compute, latency and something else to maintain. Small pipelines may not need it. If your checks fire five times a week, a person with a spreadsheet will do better. The layer pays off when the volume of noise exceeds what the team can read.
  • Keep an audit trail of dismissed differences. When the CFO asks why a flagged gap was closed, "the model said it was normal" has to come with the evidence attached.

From fire drill to background process

Month-end reconciliation is a fire drill because differences are found late and investigated from scratch. With this setup, the checks run on every load, the noise is filtered and real breaks arrive with a draft explanation. Finance spends less time waiting on the close and more time on the breaks that matter.

Pick one metric this week. Write the deterministic checks and start the resolution log. The AI layer can wait until the log has a few months of history. Truth first, explanation second.

items.title: Why Invisible Engineering Work Deserves More Recognition
items.author: Samuel Oladipupo
items.content:
By day I build hospital software. Most of what I do will never be seen by anyone outside my team: a fix to a data import that quietly stopped failing, a migration that went so smoothly nobody remembers it happened, a review comment that stopped a bad pattern spreading. By evening I write in public. A post takes me a few hours and can reach more people in a day than my best code will ever touch directly.

Only one of those shows up when someone searches my name. So which one is the real work?

It is tempting to pick a side, and plenty of people do, loudly. I think both sides are partly right, and the more interesting question sits underneath them. Researchers have been poking at that question for decades, in car factories, hospitals, universities and open source mailing lists, and what they found is more useful than either side's slogan.

The case for the buried builder

Some of the most important engineering work is invisible by design. When it goes well, nothing happens. No outage, no incident, no story to tell. The engineer who spends three weeks making a payment flow idempotent has prevented a disaster that will never be written about, because it never occurred.

In 2001, two MIT researchers, Nelson Repenning and John Sterman, studied why process improvement programmes kept failing in manufacturing and product development. Their paper took its title from something an engineer at a car company told them: "Nobody ever gets credit for fixing problems that never happened." What they found was a loop. Organisations that rely on firefighting end up rewarding and promoting the people who save the day through heroic effort, rather than the people whose quiet improvement work means there is no fire to fight. Over time, they wrote, senior management increasingly consists of these "war heroes". The system does not just ignore prevention. It selects against it.

Healthcare has been wrestling with the same pattern. Patient safety has traditionally been managed by counting what goes wrong and stamping it out. The resilience engineering researchers Erik Hollnagel, Robert Wears and Jeffrey Braithwaite call this Safety-I, and they have argued for a shift to Safety-II: moving from making sure "as few things as possible go wrong" to making sure "as many things as possible go right". Their most quoted line deserves a spot above every engineering team's desk: given how complex the work is, "the surprise is not that things occasionally go wrong but that they go right so often." The catch, as one patient safety researcher put it, is that measuring success is harder than measuring failure. Software has the same problem. We have dashboards for incidents. We have nothing for the ten thousand ordinary days when nothing broke because someone was careful.

These developers also carry context no talk can capture. They know why the retry logic has that strange delay, which customer depends on the undocumented field, what broke the last time someone touched the scheduler. That knowledge is load-bearing, and it lives in people who rarely have time to explain it to anyone outside the building.

Ten years later it nearly happened again. XZ Utils, a compression library found on almost every Linux system, had been maintained by one person, Lasse Collin, since he wrote it in 2009. In 2022 he wrote on the project's mailing list that his ability to care had been "fairly limited mostly due to longterm mental health issues", adding: "It's also good to keep in mind that this is an unpaid hobby project." Accounts that were almost certainly fake pressured him to hand over control. A helpful new contributor, "Jia Tan", gained his trust, became a maintainer and spent the following year planting a backdoor in the software. It was caught in March 2024 by Andres Freund, a Microsoft engineer who, in his spare time, noticed the new version was using more processing than it should. One invisible worker, burnt out. Another, curious. That was the margin.

And the measurement systems around builders mostly miss it. Promotions, job offers and reputations lean on what can be seen and counted. A conference talk is countable. A follower number is countable. "The system did not fall over this year" is not, even when it is the most valuable thing that happened.

So the builders have a fair grievance. A lot of real effort goes unrecognised simply because it does not produce anything people outside the team can point to.

Invisible work is not evenly distributed

There is a second layer to the builder's grievance: who ends up doing the invisible work in the first place.

In 2019, Tanya Reilly gave a talk called "Being Glue" that named something many engineers recognised straight away. Glue work is the onboarding, the roadmap updates, the questions on design documents, the noticing of things that got dropped. It is "the less glamorous, and often less-promotable, work that needs to happen to make a team successful." Her warning was blunt. Managed deliberately, glue work builds technical leadership. Left unconscious, "it can be career limiting. It can push people into less technical roles and even out of the industry."

So "good work gets noticed eventually" is not just optimistic. It costs some people more than others.

The case for the public developer

But the dismissive version of this argument, that speakers are all talk, falls apart quickly.

Many of the developers you see on stage are deep builders. The talk exists because they solved something hard and then did a second hard thing: they made it understandable. Anyone who has tried to explain a gnarly production problem to a room of strangers knows clarity is its own skill. You have to strip the problem to its essence without lying about it, anticipate the questions, and survive the person in the third row who knows more than you.

Tanya Reilly's talk is the best example. Glue work existed long before she named it. Thousands of engineers were doing it, unseen. One person on a stage giving it a name did more to get that work recognised than years of it being done quietly. I would not call that all talk. I would call it leverage.

So the public developers have a fair point too. Teaching is work. Explaining is work. The industry would be poorer without it.

Where each side gets it wrong

Legible does not mean loud. It can be a two-line note to your manager: "I found why checkout failed under load and fixed it. It would have hit us during the next sale." That sentence turns invisible work into something a decision-maker can remember. Julia Evans made the same case in her post on keeping a "brag document": some kinds of important work are simply more memorable than others, and the fuzzy work, like improving code review culture or making on-call easier, is the most likely to slip under the radar unless you write it down.

The public developer's mistake is quieter. Visibility can slowly become the job. The talks get better while the building gets thinner. Applause starts to feel like feedback on the code, when it is really feedback on the performance. Will Larson has a word for the extreme version: "preening", doing low-impact, high-visibility work. He warns that many companies "conflate high-visibility and high-impact so strongly that they can't distinguish between preening and impact." Being public is fine. Being public about work you have stopped doing is the problem.

What the world actually measures

The world does not measure effort. It never has. It measures what it can see, and it uses proxies: talks, followers, GitHub stars, titles, the size of the company on your CV.

Visibility also compounds. In 1968 the sociologist Robert Merton described the "Matthew effect" in science: credit for joint or simultaneous discoveries flows disproportionately to people who are already famous. The rich get richer. Tech works the same way. Once you are the person who gives talks, your next talk is easier to land, your posts travel further, and your ideas get taken more seriously than the same idea from someone nobody has heard of.

Measuring harder does not fix it. When McKinsey published "Yes, you can measure software developer productivity" in 2023, Kent Beck and Gergely Orosz responded with a simple model: effort, output, outcome, impact. Their warning was that whatever you measure, people will game. Measure effort and you get busywork. Measure output and you get whatever output is easiest. Their advice was to aim for team outcomes and impact, and to use effort and output only to debug problems. It works as a test for your own work too. "I spent three weeks on the payment flow" is effort. "Duplicate charges went to zero during peak sales" is impact. Only one of those survives a promotion meeting.

So the proxies are crude. They reward the visible over the valuable. But they are not random either. Over a long career, the developers I have seen do best are rarely at either extreme. They do deep work, and then they make it legible. A design note that explains a decision. An internal write-up after an incident. A short summary for leadership that turns a technical win into a business one. Occasionally, a public post or a talk.

Translating the work without replacing it

If the skill is translation, here is what it looks like in practice, roughly from least effort to most.

Write the counterfactual. Prevention work leaves nothing behind to show, so give it something. "Without this, X would have happened, and here is how we know." That one sentence is the difference between "did some refactoring" and "removed the cause of last year's two biggest outages."

Keep a running record. A brag document, updated every couple of weeks, is not vanity. It is evidence you will not be able to reconstruct from memory at review time.

Move each piece of work one rung up the effort, output, outcome, impact ladder before you share it. Your manager can usually take it the rest of the way.

Write internally before externally. An incident write-up or design note reaches the people who decide your career and helps your team. Very often it is also a public post waiting to be edited.

If you are doing glue work, say so, out loud, to your manager. Ask whether it counts toward where you want to go. If it does not, get it recognised or hand it to a rota.

And if you are the speaker, keep a build log. Check that the thing you talk about is still something you do. If your last three talks are about work from three years ago, pay attention to that.

I do not think of any of this as self-promotion. It is closer to documentation: making sure the people who need to understand what happened actually can.

None of this is unique to software. A nurse who quietly catches medication errors is doing work that rarely appears in any report, which is exactly what the Safety-II researchers were trying to change. An accountant whose reconciliations stop a problem before the audit gets no credit for the crisis that did not happen.
