The hack did not impact users on Polymarket US, the company's newer platform for people within the United States. Polymarket runs two separate prediction markets; Polymarket US operates as a federally regulated financial exchange within the country, while the flagship Polymarket is a cryptocurrency-based platform that is banned in the United States and a number of other countries. This is not the first time that Polymarket traders have experienced losses like this. "A nearly identical vendor-compromise attack hit the platform in June, draining close to $3 million from at least 11 user wallets through the same kind of injected frontend script," reports StartupFortune.
 
Hours before Polymarket halted trading, more than $2 billion in cryptocurrency was drained from Binance wallets in just 40 minutes.

items.title: How ASML Gives the Netherlands a Strategic Advantage in Global AI
items.author: tt
items.content:
The Netherlands can influence the development of AI far beyond the size of its domestic market. The source of that influence is a specialised industrial position: the machinery and knowledge needed to manufacture advanced semiconductors. ASML places the country close to an important constraint on the expansion of computing capacity. Yet the Dutch government cannot treat the company's technology, suppliers and customers as resources available for unrestricted national use. The strategic question concerns the terms on which this commercial position can support public objectives, and the costs of doing so.

A position inside production

ASML reported €32.7 billion in net sales and €4.7 billion in research and development expenditure for 2025. Its reported system sales included 48 extreme ultraviolet lithography systems. These figures establish the scale of an industrial organisation; they do not measure Dutch state capability. A machine sold to a customer becomes part of a production process whose location, ownership and operational priorities may lie elsewhere. [1]

The distinction becomes clearer through three layers: Invention, Industrialisation and Operationalisation. Invention concerns the knowledge and technical advances that expand what AI systems and their underlying technologies can do. Industrialisation concerns the production and infrastructure that make those advances reproducible at scale. Operationalisation concerns their sustained use by organisations pursuing concrete objectives. Governance connects these layers through funding, access rules, procurement and institutional responsibility.

The Netherlands has a particularly consequential position where invention becomes industrial production. The joint ASML–imec High NA EUV laboratory, opened in Veldhoven in June 2024, gave chipmakers and equipment and materials suppliers access to a prototype scanner and associated tools. The stated purpose was preparation for manufacturing. [2] Such arrangements matter because a promising technical design becomes strategically useful only when multiple organisations can make it work reliably together.

The international foundations of Dutch influence

ASML's 2025 reporting describes a supplier network of 5,100 organisations: 1,600 in the Netherlands, 700 elsewhere in Europe, the Middle East and Africa, 1,350 in North America, and 1,450 in Asia. These are supplier counts, without weights for expenditure or technical importance. [1] They establish geographical breadth, while leaving the concentration of critical dependencies to more detailed analysis.

The company also reports that approximately 80% of its bill of materials comes from external suppliers and describes its optical collaboration with ZEISS. [3] This makes the policy problem reciprocal. Countries and firms seeking advanced manufacturing equipment depend on capabilities assembled around ASML; ASML also depends on capabilities beyond Dutch territory. Sustaining influence therefore requires cooperation with the partners whose contributions keep that position technically credible.

What the state can decide

Export authorisation provides a concrete mechanism linking commercial capability to public authority. In January 2025, the Dutch government announced an extension of its national controls to specified measuring and inspection equipment, effective from April. The announcement explained that applications would be assessed individually for destinations outside the EU and distinguished authorisation requirements from a general prohibition. [4]

This mechanism gives the state an intervention point. It does not establish control over every stage of semiconductor production or guarantee that a restriction will achieve its intended strategic result. That result depends on which technologies are covered, the availability of substitutes, enforcement and the decisions of other supplier countries. Judging Dutch influence requires examining these conditions rather than inferring political power directly from company revenue.

The same state also has to maintain the conditions for production at home. Project Beethoven, announced in March 2024, committed a €2.51 billion package to the semiconductor ecosystem, including education, accessibility, housing and spatial infrastructure. The government explicitly connected the package to keeping the Netherlands attractive for ASML's investment. [5] This was an announced policy commitment; its financial scale alone does not demonstrate completed delivery or resolved bottlenecks.

From industrial importance to usable capability

For Dutch ministries and public organisations, the operational question remains separate: which AI capabilities can they access, maintain and use for their own tasks? Hosting an influential equipment producer does not automatically provide a ministry with dependable computing capacity, suitable models or the staff needed to integrate them into public services. Those connections require decisions and budgets of their own.

There is an industrial route to deeper capability. ASML describes the use of AI in engineering, computational lithography and maintenance in its 2025 reporting. [3] This illustrates how knowledge generated within a production ecosystem can also improve its operations. The national opportunity is conditional: research partnerships, training and procurement must help relevant expertise circulate while respecting commercial knowledge and security requirements. The benefits cannot be assumed to spread throughout the economy unaided.

What would change the assessment

Four observable developments would clarify the Netherlands' trajectory. First, changes in licensing decisions and equipment deliveries would reveal how export policy affects actual access. Second, disclosures on critical supplier capacity and substitution would show whether international dependence is becoming more manageable. Third, completed education, housing and infrastructure measures would indicate whether Project Beethoven is relieving the constraints it identified. Fourth, documented public and industrial AI deployments would show whether technical strength is translating into sustained organisational performance.

The Netherlands can remain an influential partner in the governance and supply of advanced production technologies. That role depends on preserving the engineering ecosystem while making selective, credible decisions about access. Its strongest strategic asset is the ability to participate in decisions others cannot easily disregard. Converting that position into broader national capability requires work beyond the semiconductor equipment industry itself.

This is original country analysis applying the GOAI capability conversion framework. It is not a peer-reviewed country assessment or a scored ranking. Proposed applications and indicators are analytical judgments; company and government claims are attributed to their sources.

All sources were accessed on 20 October 2026. Corporate and government statements are identified as such in the text.

items.title: Trump's CTFC Steps In to Defend Kalshi As Utah Brings Criminal Charges Against Execs
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has sued Utah to defend its claimed exclusive authority over federally registered prediction markets, as the state files (PDF) 14 criminal charges against Kalshi and its co-founders for allegedly violating anti-gambling laws. The Verge reports: On Wednesday, Utah's Attorney General Derek Brown filed charges against Kalshi co-founders Tarek Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara, including 12 counts of online gambling promotion, a third-degree felony, one count of a pattern of unlawful activity, a second-degree felony, and general gambling promotion, a Class A misdemeanor. The civil lawsuit calls Kalshi a "back-alley gambling den," and Attorney General Brown didn't mince words in a statement to Gizmodo.
 
"Gambling is illegal in Utah, whether you place the bet, run the game, or promote it. Calling it a 'prediction market' doesn't change what it is, and being federally registered doesn't put a company above the law," said Brown. "A federal court has already ruled that Utah's gambling laws apply to Kalshi," continued Brown. "Kalshi kept taking bets from Utahns anyway. That is illegal, and we're putting a stop to it."
 
[...] The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has been jumping into action to protect Kalshi and Polymarket by filing lawsuits against any state that brings charges against the betting sites. President Trump's son, Donald Trump Jr., is a paid advisor to both companies. The CFTC announced Wednesday that it was suing the state of Utah as part of its "commitment to maintaining its exclusive jurisdiction over CFTC-registered prediction markets." The argument is that the feds alone should be regulating these sites.
 
"Utah seeks to shut down prediction markets across a wide variety of markets," CFTC Chairman Michael S. Selig said in a statement. "Event contracts do not just serve hedging and investment purposes -- they also provide the public with information about the outcome of future events. Congress entrusted the CFTC to be the federal regulator with sole responsibility to oversee these markets," continued Selig. "As I've said before, the CFTC has the expertise and responsibility to defend its exclusive jurisdiction over commodity derivatives, and that's exactly what we'll do."

items.title: Your Billing Migration is Really a State Machine
items.author: naresh goyal
items.content:
A customer opens their inbox and finds two invoices for the same subscription. Another customer shows up in the retention report as a churn, except they never cancelled. Their payment failed, the subscription lapsed in the billing system, and the lapse got recorded as a lost customer.

I led the architecture on a migration that produced both of these bugs. A large file-sharing company was replacing its homegrown quoting and billing system with Salesforce CPQ and Salesforce Billing, integrated with Oracle ERP, across hundreds of thousands of customer accounts. The data moved fine. State was the problem.

I’m Naresh Goyal, a Salesforce and GTM systems architect with 20+ years in CPQ, billing, and revenue systems. I hold the Revenue Cloud Advanced certification and led the architecture on the migration in this story.

Alongside revenue systems work, I've been focused on bringing AI into go-to-market teams. I led AI deployment across a GTM organization, built an AI orchestration platform for revenue workflows, and set up a Salesforce MCP integration with Claude so agents can work directly with CRM data. That work keeps reinforcing the same lesson as this migration: AI agents are only as reliable as the state they read.

I’m sharing these lessons because billing migrations usually fail quietly, and most fixes only surface in postmortems.

A subscription does not live in one system. Quoting knows what was sold. Billing knows what was invoiced and paid. Provisioning knows what the customer can access. The ERP knows what revenue was recognized. Each system holds a partial copy of the truth, and each one updates on its own schedule.

When those copies disagree, the bug lands on a customer. Billing treats a subscription as active and keeps invoicing it after provisioning has shut off access. Or the reverse. The failures we kept hitting were duplicate invoices for one subscription, churn records for customers whose only problem was a failed payment, and provisioning that fired at the wrong moment, granting access before payment was confirmed or withholding it after.

None of these are data movement bugs. The records arrived. They arrived carrying state that the receiving system read differently.

Our fix started on a whiteboard. Every subscription got an explicit state machine: named states and the allowed transitions between them. Draft, quoted, ordered, activated, suspended, amended, expired, cancelled. A subscription could move from ordered to activated. It could not jump from quoted to invoiced, and any process that tried got rejected instead of quietly writing a bad state.

This sounds basic, and most billing systems never do it. State ends up implied by a status field here, a checkbox there, a date that may or may not be set. When state is implied, every integration invents its own reading of it, and you ship the disagreements to your customers.

Here is a simplified version of the transition table. The important column is the last one.

Order recognized by finance

Upsell or downgrade quoted

Amendment order recognized

Term ends without renewal

Notice that "payment failed" moves a subscription to Suspended, not Cancelled. That row addresses the false churn problem from the opening. Churn reporting counts Cancelled and Expired, never Suspended, so a failed card no longer looks like a lost customer.

Do this on your own migration: list the states, list the transitions, and name the one system allowed to make each transition. If two systems can both push a subscription into the same state, you have found a future incident.

The sharpest disagreement sat between billing and provisioning. The legacy setup triggered provisioning off the sales process: a deal closed, a webhook fired, access followed. A closed deal is a sales opinion. The financial system had not yet recognized the order, and sometimes it never did.

We rebuilt the handshake around an event. Provisioning fires only when the order product reaches the Activated state, the point where the financial system officially recognizes the order. The trigger is the state change itself. No timer. No scheduled job guessing. No sales stage.

Access granted before payment and access denied after payment look like opposite bugs. They have the same root cause: provisioning listening to the wrong signal. Bind it to the financial state and both failure modes close.

Before any configuration began, we profiled the full source data, and it was humbling. Thousands of accounts were ghosts. Some had no opportunities at all. Some held closed deals with no products attached. Account hierarchies pointed at parent accounts that no longer existed.

Migrating that as-is would have carried every one of those problems into the new platform, where each would have surfaced as a migration defect and burned the team's credibility in the first week. We stopped, cleaned the accounts and repaired the hierarchies with the revenue operations team, and only then started loading.

Your source data is worse than you think. The time to find out is before the new system exists, while cleanup is still a data exercise instead of a production incident. If you want a checklist for that first pass, the three questions to ask before any data migration is a good place to start.

We did not flip the whole company in one weekend. During the cutover window, the legacy system stayed read-only while both systems stayed in sync. Downstream consumers then switched one at a time: finance first, then provisioning, then the customer success tools. Before each switch, a validation checkpoint compared both systems on the records that the consumer cared about.

A phased cutover turns one giant risk into a series of small, checkable ones. When a checkpoint fails, you know which consumer and which record class broke, and the legacy system is still there to compare against. For the checkpoints themselves, this account of proving a 12-million-record migration correct shows what real source-to-target reconciliation looks like

Historical records carry commercial terms from deals signed years ago. New pricing rules know nothing about those deals. Run a migrated contract through a new pricing engine, and it can reprice a renewal under rules that did not exist when the customer signed.

We put a bypass flag on every migrated quote, opportunity, and order. Pricing and product rules check the flag and skip those records, which keep their original terms through a separate legacy price book. New business runs through the live pricing engine. History stays history. It is one more case of a lesson CPQ teams learned long ago: the pricing engine is only as good as the catalog and data underneath it.

Revenue schedules were the last piece, because finance owns them and finance does not accept assurances. We migrated the in-progress schedules into rules-based recognition, then ran the old and new systems side by side. The final cutover happened only after consecutive clean cycles, with finance signing off on each one.

If your migration touches revenue recognition, build the parallel run into the plan from the start, with a named sign-off at the end of it. It is slower. It is also the only version of that cutover that survives an audit conversation.

If you are planning a billing or subscription migration, spend your design time on state. Write the state machine. Decide which system owns each transition. Bind provisioning to the financial event. Profile and clean the source before you configure anything. Cut over in phases with checkpoints, wall history off from new pricing logic, and let finance call the revenue cutover.

Once those decisions are made, the data load is close to a weekend job. The decisions are the migration.

items.title: Patrick Stewart, 'Star Trek' Captain and 'X-Men' Superhero, Dies At 86
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Slashdot readers Cpt_Kirks, eklektic, sconeu, and Vrallis share the unfortunate news of Patrick Stewart's passing. Longtime spokesperson Kelly Bush Novak said Stewart died Wednesday at the age of 86 at his home in Los Angeles following "a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia."
 
"He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all," Bush Novak wrote. "We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace."
 
The acclaimed British actor became a science-fiction icon as Capt. Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation and Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men films. Beyond those iconic roles, Stewart earned multiple Emmy and Golden Globe nominations for performances in Moby Dick, The Lion in Winter, Extras, Hamlet, and Blunt Talk. He later returned to his most famous role in Star Trek: Picard.

items.title: The Zombies of Tech: What Actually Powers the World
items.author: William
items.content:
In Week 9 of the IBM Full-Stack JavaScript Developer track, I stepped back from tutorials and asked a different question: what is the internet actually running on?

The answer isn’t the framework that trended on X this morning. It’s older, quieter, and far more stubborn.

COBOL: the 67-year-old that moves your money. Created in 1959, COBOL is still widely estimated to sit behind about 95% of ATM transactions and 80% of in-person banking transactions, with some 220 billion lines in production and around $3 trillion in commerce a day. One example: back in 2012, Bank of New York Mellon reported maintaining 112,500 COBOL programs, about 343 million lines of code. The catch is a talent gap. Universities largely stopped teaching it decades ago, and banks are now experimenting with AI tools to help maintain and modernize it.

PHP and WordPress: the web’s workhorse. PHP is used by about 70% of websites whose server-side language is known. WordPress, built on it, runs roughly 42% of all websites.

jQuery: declared dead, still everywhere. It’s on about 67% of all websites. Even jQuery 1.x, a version from the 2000s, is still found on around 13%.

Linux: the invisible foundation. About 62% of websites with an identifiable OS run Linux, and the broader Unix family covers around 92%. Every system on the TOP500 supercomputer list runs Linux too.

And the new stuff earns its place. React Native isn’t legacy, but it shows why tools survive: Shopify moved its flagship app to it and now shares about 86% of its code across iOS and Android, up from roughly 5%. Efficiency like that is why a tool lasts.

the technologies that last aren’t the newest; they’re the ones that are reliable, and rewriting something that works is expensive and risky. As a developer, learning the new tools matters, but so does respecting the old systems that keep running.

What’s the oldest piece of tech you’ve seen still running in production?

Sources: W3Techs (2026), Reuters (2017), Computerworld (2012), Shopify’s React Native migration. Usage figures cover only sites where the technology is detectable.

items.title: Beyond Price, What Gives Bitcoin Its Value?
items.author: Evan Ceolini
items.content:
Bitcoin began its history back in the distant 2008–2009. During this time, it managed to transform from an obscure digital currency that was once used to buy pizza into a highly liquid asset. Although the basic principles of Bitcoin have remained the same, its price has changed dramatically during this period.

Just a year ago, in October 2025, one BTC was worth about $126,080. And a year later, at the end of October 2026, its price fell by almost 36% — to $81,000. Such “ups and downs” are an interesting phenomenon for me as the CEO of a crypto aggregator. Bitcoin became the starting point for the development of the modern crypto industry, and its price movements influence the mood and dynamics of the entire market.

In this article, I’ll look beyond the price chart to explore what gives Bitcoin its value, what drives demand for BTC, and why its role in the crypto market goes far beyond its latest price movements.

Value and price answer different questions

The value of Bitcoin is an individual story. For example, two different people may explain what it consists of in different ways. Someone doesn’t want to use traditional banks for payments or transfers and therefore uses Bitcoin. For another person, it’s more important to have a “reliable” crypto asset with a history and limited supply in their crypto portfolio. These cases are small illustrations of how Bitcoin can be used and what it’s valued for.

But value and price are different things. The quoted price is just the price that the buyer and seller come to in each individual trade. One seller takes what the buyer offers, and the next trade may be at a different price. There is no hidden agreed value in dollars behind the quote that you're meant to be able to work out.

Thus, it is more difficult to evaluate Bitcoin than a traditional financial asset. Unlike stocks, Bitcoin does not entitle you to any future earnings of a company, nor are there any future cash flows that can be used to determine its value. According to Fidelity, is all about supply and demand. However, that doesn't provide a clear 'fair value' figure.

What supports Bitcoin's value

Since 2012, Bitcoin has undergone a approximately every four years, reducing the block subsidy by 50% every 210,000 blocks. Following the April 2024 halving, the subsidy fell to 3.125 BTC per block, down from the initial 50 BTC.

What does this tell us? Bitcoin has a capped supply of approximately 21 million coins, while the rate of new BTC issuance declines with each halving. However, as Eswar Prasad argues in his article, , scarcity alone is unlikely to be a sufficient source of value. I agree with this view.

. The block subsidy is determined by the protocol rules and block height, rather than by the discretionary decisions of a centralized issuer. Anyone considering buying BTC can examine these rules to understand how the issuance of new coins is expected to change over time.

This allows you to take halving into account when assessing the market, but it doesn’t allow you to predict price movements. A reduction in the rate of new BTC issuance alone doesn’t guarantee an increase in Bitcoin’s value: much depends on demand and other market factors. Therefore, when making a decision to buy, it’s important to consider not only the issuance rate but also the possible risks.

2. Decentralization and сontrol

The Bitcoin blockchain is so that transactions and blocks are independently verified by network participants. Miners use Proof of Work to propose new blocks, while full nodes check whether those blocks comply with Bitcoin’s protocol rules. Proof of Work makes it costly to rewrite transaction history, which helps protect the integrity of the network and makes it reliable for transferring value.

This differs from Arbitrum, which has a different governance structure. Its Security Council has specific emergency powers that allow it to intervene in the network, as demonstrated by the in which it moved ~30,766 ETH held by the KelpDAO to a frozen address. Bitcoin has no equivalent council with the authority to carry out such an intervention.

For me, the important distinction is that . Each participant can verify the rules for themselves, but no single participant can unilaterally control the entire network.

3. Infrastructure and liquidity

Why do we need money if you can’t buy anything with it? The same goes for Bitcoin. Since its inception, an infrastructure has gradually formed around BTC that allows you not only to store it, but also to buy, sell, and use it for transfers and payments. For example:

Of course, as a result, Bitcoin has become much more accessible through exchanges, payment systems, and regulated investment products. But I want to emphasize one important thing: The market quote and the price at which a transaction is actually executed on a specific exchange or exchange service are not the same thing. Liquidity depends on the size of the transaction, market depth, the specific platform, and current market conditions.

Is the ‘Digital gold’ argument reasonable?

Bitcoin is often compared to gold. For instance, Larry Fink, CEO of BlackRock, has Bitcoin as a way of “digitizing gold.” The arguments in favor of this comparison tend to echo the points I mentioned above. sums them up by pointing to Bitcoin’s scarcity, portability, and divisibility. I think gold works well as a metaphor for explaining Bitcoin’s value, rather than its price, to someone outside the crypto industry.

But when it comes to price, the comparison becomes more complicated. Gold has a much longer history as a store of value. In an , the World Gold Council highlighted the difference in price volatility: Bitcoin’s annualized volatility was around 60%, compared with approximately 15% for gold. These figures were based on daily returns in US dollars from December 31, 2018, to December 31, 2023.

Why the price moves faster than the network

A coin mined years ago can come onto the market today, that’s why the supply of BTC on the market depends not only on the issuance of new coins but also on the decisions of current holders. You can sell the BTC you bought in an earlier cycle, or you can simply hold on to it.

That is precisely why we should not attribute the price increase solely to the halving, since the schedule only answers some of the questions. While we can anticipate changes in issuance volume, we cannot predict how many holders will sell their coins during a price rally, nor how much money buyers will invest. But this isn’t the only factor influencing the movement of the BTC price. I would also highlight other historical events:

  • Monetary policy has an impact on the cost of borrowing and the options available to those holding cash. In 2022, the went from 0–0.25% to 4.25–4.50%, and Bitcoin lost 64.2% (). In other words, 2022 seems to disprove the notion that Bitcoin is immune to the influence of the traditional financial system. We can't actually say how much of that loss was attributable to Fed policy.
  • Access can also be had via the regulator's own decision. When the SEC approved the 2024 ETP listings, they explicitly . A product could be sold through that route without the regulator having to certify that Bitcoin was fairly priced. I'd be very wary of treating regulatory access as a guarantee as to what you should pay.
  • A trader using leverage can control a position which is larger than their own capital. If their collateral is insufficient, then the position may be liquidated. looks at exactly what happens when a string of forced trades hit a thin book with wide spreads.

These examples show why Bitcoin's predictable supply schedule is only one part of the picture. Its market price also reflects monetary conditions, regulatory developments, and trading activity.

What exactly historical episodes show

Near $19,400 in December 2017, about $3,700 at the end of 2018 (). futures launched in December 2017 ().

New trading instruments can expand market access without preventing speculative excess or subsequent price corrections.

Financing conditions and failures of intermediaries matter alongside protocol design.

US spot Bitcoin ETP approval (). Bitcoin's annual gain was 121.5% ().

New access channels can change demand without changing the asset's basic rules.

Amberdata recorded $6.93 billion in crypto liquidations within 40 minutes ().

Forced position closures can amplify a market shock.

2017 and 2018 showed the limits of access

gave the traders another tool. It didn't in any way give the holders protection against a reversal. I wouldn't blame the subsequent fall on the CME simply because it came after the launch.

Terra and FTX are in any account or story about 2022 (alongside the rise in interest rates). goes into detail about how the collapse of both of those businesses had a knock-on effect for others.

For Bitcoin holders, dependence on a custodian or a borrower of coins was a real problem. A company that was lending out your BTC was exposing those coins to the risk of the borrower failing to repay. The borrower was, of course, under an obligation to repay. That obligation wasn't just a function of the Bitcoin network producing valid blocks on the blockchain. That's why I draw a clear distinction between the security of the network and the reliability of a business that holds your coins.

Figure 3. US federal funds target range for 2022 (annual daily series). Lower and upper limits, percent. Sources: Federal Reserve via FRED,and DFEDTARU. This is a chart of policy timing, not a chart of a measured causal effect on Bitcoin.

2024 changed the channels through which demand arrived

In 2024, two things that were often mentioned in conjunction actually did quite different things.

The ETP provided people with a new way to get exposure via securities, while they reduced the amount of new issuance. To treat them as one explanation for the year's return doesn't really explain how much of the buying was via the new channel.

To work that out, you'd look at fund subscriptions and redemptions. A higher AUM figure isn't necessarily indicative of new money having come in from investors. The AUM could be higher simply because the BTC that the fund already holds has gone up in value.

October 2025 exposed the speed of forced repricing

also looked at the orders that were sitting in the market during the October 2025 liquidations. With fewer orders and wider spreads, traders who were forced to exit their positions found themselves in much worse execution conditions. Selling into that market would have added to the fall.

The total in the table is for crypto positions (not just BTC), and it's not a measure of an equivalent amount of capital permanently withdrawn from BTC. I take it to be a measure of forced position closures over the period that Amberdata was looking at.

Quantum risk: a long-term challenge for Bitcoin

A more fundamental objection to Bitcoin is of course the risk to the cryptography that underpins ownership. If a holder no longer has confidence in that cryptography, then they have a reason to doubt the asset itself, irrespective of the current state of the market.

On 15th October 2026, Google Quantum AI reported on its Willow processor. Magic state cultivation is a technique which produces the low-error quantum states required for fault-tolerant computation and could in principle reduce the amount of hardware required for some computations. Google notes that it still needs to demonstrate the technique at scale.

Google's that are powerful enough to break elliptic curve signatures, which authorise spending. This is the real threat, separate from the October lab result. Benzinga's report (as repeated by ) clearly distinguished between a potential future vulnerability and an attack that could be carried out today. The hardware experiment did not demonstrate that Bitcoin had been cracked.

Before calling Bitcoin a good long-term investment, we need to understand how this risk will be managed. Quantum-resistant signatures would have to be in the network rules and in the wallet software, and people would have to adopt them. I wouldn’t simply assume that all users will join this initiative just because there is a financial incentive to protect the network.

My view on what makes Bitcoin valuable

It’s important to understand that it’s the first cryptocurrency, which laid the foundation for the development of the entire subsequent crypto industry. Today, smart contracts and decentralized applications are being developed on the basis of blockchain technologies.

But for me, the value of Bitcoin lies in something else as well. It’s important to me that the network isn’t controlled by a single organization or corporation, but operates on the basis of a decentralized protocol, the rules of which participants can verify independently.

Furthermore, Bitcoin is gaining increasing recognition from institutional investors and large businesses. It is no longer just some kind of internet coin, but an asset that has become part of the traditional financial system.

Bitcoin is also the first asset I look at when I want to get a sense of the crypto market's mood. It was the first crypto to achieve global prominence. A found an average return correlation of 0.52 between Bitcoin and the other crypto assets from Jan 2018 to Mar 2023. That doesn't mean every other asset moves in line with Bitcoin, of course, but it does give me a reason to use Bitcoin as a benchmark for market sentiment.

Author’s note: This article is for informational purposes only and does not constitute financial, investment, legal, or tax advice. Digital assets and DeFi protocols involve significant risks, including loss of principal. Rates, liquidity, availability, and product terms may change, and access may be restricted by jurisdiction. Readers should conduct their own research and assess the applicable terms and risks before using any product or protocol.

items.title: Adapting a SwiftUI Courier App for iPhone Duo's Foldable Display
items.author: Philip Ellis
items.content:
Our courier app launched on the iPhone Duo simulator but there was no back button on the Messages screen. The details sheet covered the navigation controls. On a map, part of the route could easily be out of view.

These were gaps in our app. We wanted to fix them before marking the app ready for the Duo. Much of the work involved how our existing interface worked in a differently-shaped window. Once the map, sheets and navigation started to play well together, we could produce a screenshot of the app for the App Store in an unfolded state.

In our driver screens we show a route on a map, delivery details, messages and actions for proof of delivery. On a narrow iPhone, a bottom sheet lets the driver switch between the details and the map. On the Duo, both could be shown at once.

Opening the app was the beginning

In this wider view, the relationship between the views changed. At times, the system would present the sheet next to the map. And navigation buttons could appear in a space occupied by the sheet. In the narrow view, we had assumptions about this layout. They no longer held up.

We started this work using the iOS 27.1 Duo simulator and Xcode 27.1 beta tooling. The observations below are of that tooling, not necessarily of every release of Xcode or of every piece of Duo hardware.

We didn't save the version of the beta build used to take our screenshots. You could check Apple's release notes for Xcode 27.1 and test for tooling issues in that version.

Work out where the sheet actually is

In our first pass at this, we used size classes to work out whether the sheet would be docked. In three places in our code we guessed at that.

But a size class doesn't tell us where the sheet might end up. It's up to the system whether to present the sheet on one side of the map. We wanted the content of the sheet, the map and navigation to all agree on the layout.

Instead of guessing, we took a measurement of the sheet and the map. And we compared the horizontal position of the sheet with the bounds of the map.

struct SheetPlacement: Equatable {
    var map: ClosedRange<CGFloat>?
    var sheet: ClosedRange<CGFloat>?

    var isDocked: Bool {
        guard let map, let sheet else { return false }
        let width = map.upperBound - map.lowerBound
        return sheet.lowerBound - map.lowerBound > width / 4
            && map.upperBound - sheet.upperBound < 32
    }
}

Each view reports its frame through SwiftUI’s onGeometryChange modifier. We compare the horizontal bounds of the sheet and map to determine whether the sheet is docked. So if you pull up or down on a bottom sheet, our decision about whether to dock it doesn't change.

Put the back button where the driver can reach it

The thresholds support our sheet-and-map layout. They aren't part of a broader SwiftUI docking system. Most importantly, we now provided the same answer about the position of the sheet to each of the views involved.

Most obviously, this broke Messages. In our unfolded state, we showed a rail on the trailing edge of the navigation bar. When the sheet docked, it covered this rail (including the back button).

A screen can feel open, yet still be limiting for the user. We wanted the same map and navigation actions regardless of where the sheet appeared.

When the sheet is docked, we hide the navigation bar. But we add those actions over the top-leading corner of the map. When the sheet returns to the bottom, we restore the normal navigation bar.

.toolbar(placement.isDocked ? .hidden : .automatic,
         for: .navigationBar)
.overlay(alignment: .topLeading) {
    if placement.isDocked {
        controls()
            .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: .leading)
            .padding(.trailing, placement.trailingInset)
    }
}

This inset on the trailing edge represents how much of the screen the docked sheet would occupy. That way, the driver could see some of the map and the controls.

And we made the controls respond to Dynamic Type. ViewThatFits first shows them in a single row. But as the available space shrinks, it pushes the actions on the map into a second row.

Even on a wide device, there may not be enough room for the controls once we add the sheet and larger text. So we included a medium height on our bottom sheet. That way the driver could see details of the sheet while still seeing some of the map.

Give a side sheet useful states

It didn't make sense to include this option when the sheet was docked. The map was already visible next to it. And at half height, the content of the sheet got cut off.

So we dropped the medium detent when the sheet was docked. In the bottom sheet layout, we leave it up to the content.

And we needed to add a transition. If the sheet was at medium height when it docked, taking away that option could leave it in a collapsed state. So in our sheet, we moved that selection to the expanded state. The driver shouldn't need to re-open the details if the size of the window changed.

This was a subtle change to the state of our sheet, but one that affected its appearance. Now the options in our sheet depend on its placement. And when the sheet moves from one placement to another, we preserve useful actions.

Frame the route in the space that remains

The map required two changes. First, the size of the window wasn't the same as the area we could use for the route. The docked sheet covered the trailing side of the map.

We add trailing safe-area padding to the map based on the docked sheet’s width. This keeps the route framed in the visible area while the map continues to draw behind the sheet.

Second, when we unfold, fold, rotate or dock a sheet, the visible area changes. MapKit could keep its camera across these sizes. And the route could well fall out of view.

We check the size of the map and its safe area. We cancel any pending refit of the map and wait 300ms for the layout to complete. Then we refit the route.

refitTask?.cancel()
refitTask = Task {
    try? await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(300))
    guard !Task.isCancelled else { return }
    var transaction = Transaction()
    transaction.disablesAnimations = true
    withTransaction(transaction) { cameraPosition = .automatic }
    await Task.yield()
    withAnimation(.easeInOut(duration: 0.3)) {
        cameraPosition = .region(region)
    }
}

Why do we clear the camera? Well, if we applied the same region, we might do nothing. And 300ms was something we added, not required by the platform.

Taken together, the refit and inset allow the route to reflect what the driver could see in the window. Just changing the size of the window wasn't sufficient.

Keep the checks about using the app

With these changes we could check, for example, whether after unfolding the window, the driver could see the route, read its details, access the actions on the map and get back from Messages.

We also need to check larger text and switch layouts while a sheet is already open. Launching directly into a wide window can miss problems with the camera position or sheet selection during a resize.

In our Android Fold work, I found a bottom sheet in the middle of the screen could hide the route on a wide window. We changed the layout so the details would appear next to the map. That change required decisions about space. So did many of the ones I made in my app.

In its October 28 announcement of the new MacBook Pro with a touchscreen, Apple suggested developers could try touch interactions in their iPadOS and iOS apps on this display. We haven't tested our app on this hardware. For an app that runs on Mac, we'd check the same sheet and navigation behavior with pointer, keyboard, and touch input.

Then capture the layout for the App Store

Once we'd fixed my app, we could have taken screenshots of its behavior on the unfolded screen. To do that, our capture tools needed workarounds.

In our beta testing, XCUIScreen.main picked the cover display even when the inner panel was in use. Our fastlane helper selected the largest nonblank image from all the screens.

let screenshot = XCUIScreen.screens
    .map { $0.screenshot() }
    .sorted { area($0.image) > area($1.image) }
    .first { !isBlank($0.image) }
    ?? XCUIScreen.main.screenshot()

In our setup, the inactive display produced a black image. For our fixture scenes, choosing the largest nonblank image let us select the active display’s screenshot. We also checked capture dimensions to reject images from the wrong display.

After rebooting, the simulator lost its unfolded posture. To work around this, we wrote a watcher that restored the unfolded posture after reboot.

We launched our app directly into fixture scenes because test taps could reach the cover display instead of the visible panel. This made captures repeatable, but didn't replace testing user navigation. But this didn't eliminate the value of testing navigation in the app for someone using it.

In its screenshot specs (check as of October 28) Apple does allow 2853 x 2007 or 2007 x 2853 images of the unfolded screen. Our capture tool rotates and resizes the image for use in the landscape slot.

Apple says from April 2027, apps using the iOS 27.1 SDK or later will need Duo screenshots.

The screenshots showed the result of the app fixes: reachable controls, sheet states suited to their placement, and a route framed in the visible map area.

Before you take screenshots of your own Duo, go into key screens for your app and move the window around them. What gets selected, what moves and what doesn't? These checks helped us find the fixes we needed before submitting our screenshots and getting our app up to date with a first class Duo experience.

items.title: It's Time for Generative AI to Prioritize Understanding Over Communication
items.author: Kelvin Leong
items.content:
Past communication tech conquered physical distance and time. But as generative AI becomes part of how we create, receive, and interpret human messages, it must focus not just on speed and ease, but on reducing the emotional and interpretive distance between people.

Communication is one of the most basic human survival behaviors. People communicate to warn others about danger, ask for help, share knowledge, coordinate actions, build relationships, solve conflicts, and make decisions. In modern society, almost every form of collective activity depends on communication: scientific research, business cooperation, education, government operations, family life, and even an ordinary conversation between friends.

Therefore, communication has never been only about transmitting information.

If communication were simply about moving information from Point A to Point B, then a fax machine would already have solved most human problems.

Unfortunately, humans are not fax machines.

The deeper purpose of communication is to meet human needs. We need to understand the environment around us, and we also need to understand the people around us. We want other people to understand our intentions, needs, and concerns. At the same time, we must work with people whose knowledge, interests, values, and life experiences may be completely different from our own.

So communication looks simple, but in reality it is extremely complex.

At the most basic level, the structure of communication is so simple: a sender creates a message, a medium carries it, and a receiver receives and interprets it. For decades, this has been one of the central structures in communication theory.

The problem is that two sides of this process are human. And once human beings are involved, things are no longer simple. The sender has their own background, knowledge, motivation, emotional state, culture, and understanding of the situation. Meanwhile, the receiver brings an entirely different set of perspectives, which rarely align completely. The sender may believe a message is perfectly clear because, in their mind, ten underlying assumptions need no explanation. However, the receiver cannot automatically know those unstated assumptions. A word that sounds completely neutral to one person may carry strong emotional weight for another. Humor can be interpreted as playful or as disrespect. Similarly, silence might signal agreement, hesitation, uncertainty, or rejection.

Communication technology, as a medium, has been most successful in solving is physical separation.

Reducing physical distance

For most of human history, physical distance was the enemy of communication. The speed of a message depended on how fast a person could travel, how fast a horse could run, how fast a ship could sail, or how quickly a document could be delivered.

Modern communication technologies gradually removed this barrier. The telegraph allowed information to cross long distances through electricity for the first time. The telephone allowed human voices to cross distance in real time. Later, computer networks such as ARPANET connected people, machines, and information systems on a larger scale. The World Wide Web then made information stored in different computers and institutions easier to connect and share. After that, email, mobile phones, social media, instant messaging, and videoconferencing made communication faster, cheaper, and more widely available.

Today, people across several continents can work together, attend meetings, exchange information, and even maintain long-term relationships, while the delay may be only one or two seconds. From this point of view, communication technology has been very successful in reducing physical distance. But one problem has never been fully solved. Distance has been reduced, but misunderstanding has not disappeared.

The reason is not difficult to understand: the most difficult barrier in communication has never been only the distance between two places, but also the distance between two minds.

With the arrival of generative AI, the difference between physical distance and mental understanding has suddenly become even more important.

Today, people already use generative AI to write emails, prepare meeting summaries, rewrite messages, translate text, adjust tone, explain ideas, and suggest how to reply to others. This creates a basic difference between generative AI and most earlier communication technologies. Telephones, email, and videoconferencing mainly transmit messages created by people. Their job is to move something from one side to another.

Generative AI is not only a delivery worker, it also begins to help write the letter. It can help create, modify, and even interpret messages. Hancock, Naaman, and Levy define “AI-mediated communication” as a form of communication in which an intelligent agent modifies, improves, or generates messages on behalf of a communicator.

In other words, generative AI can enter both the sending and receiving sides of communication. It can help people overcome language barriers, simplify difficult information, summarize discussions, and identify unanswered questions. These functions are clearly valuable, but this also makes communication more complex.

Social media greatly expanded access to information, communities, and public expression. However, greater access did not automatically lead to greater understanding.

People interpret information through their own experiences, identities, values, knowledge, and beliefs. This individual perspective does not mean selfishness; it simply means that no two people understand the world from exactly the same position.

One example is confirmation bias, the tendency to seek or interpret information in ways that support existing beliefs. Social media can make this tendency easier to express through choices about whom to follow, which communities to join, and which sources to ignore. Recommendation systems can further shape what users see and may contribute to information bubbles and echo chambers. Research shows that both algorithms and user choices can affect exposure to different perspectives, while similar patterns of selective exposure have been observed across other platforms.

It would be too simple to argue that social media algorithms created confirmation bias or individualism. They did not. Human beings already had different interests, beliefs, and social identities. The main lesson from social media is that technology can amplify human bias.

If the problem of social media is that it helps people select information that matches their existing views, then the problem created by generative AI may go one step further: it may make communication itself more self-centered.

Prompt engineering is often described as a way to improve the quality of AI output. This is not wrong but better prompts do not automatically remove the user’s own bias. Instead, they may turn unclear biases, assumptions, and positions into clearer, more precise, and more persuasive instructions. In fact, generative AI can produce a very strong argument in support of the user’s original position, but that does not mean the user understands the other side any better. Research by Cheng and colleagues supports this concern. They found that sycophantic AI systems may excessively agree with users in interpersonal situations, making users more confident that they are right while reducing their willingness to take actions that may help repair conflict.

The word ‘generative’ should therefore receive more attention when we think about AI-supported communication.

If the internet accelerated how fast we deliver thoughts, generative AI accelerates how fast we produce them. Generative AI can greatly improve productivity, but it can also accelerate miscommunication. This problem matters because failures in communication are not minor technical errors.

Many problems in human life can be traced, at least partly, to failures of communication. A misunderstanding between friends can become a long-term conflict because neither person clarifies the original meaning. Repeated communication failure can damage family relationships. Poorly expressed criticism can cause emotional harm that lasts far longer than the conversation itself. In organizations, communication failures can lead to incorrect requirements, duplicated work, weak coordination, and poor decisions. A senior manager may receive a clear presentation without realizing that different teams disagree about the meaning of the underlying data. A company may issue a technically accurate public statement that fails to recognize how customers will interpret it, resulting in a public-relations crisis. In scientific and public communication, misunderstanding can be even more serious. Differences between what scientists mean by terms such as risk, evidence, significant, or uncertainty and what members of the public understand from the same words can affect trust and decision-making.

These examples return us to the starting point of this argument: communication exists to serve human needs.

If people communicate faster but understand each other less, a central purpose of communication has not been achieved.

The next challenge: reducing emotional and interpretive distance

Communication technologies of the past achieved remarkable success in overcoming physical barriers. Distance became less important. Time barriers became smaller. Transmission costs continued to fall.

The next important goal for generative AI should be to reduce emotional and interpretive distance. Emotional and interpretive distance means the invisible gap between what one person truly wants to communicate and what another person finally understands.

By emotional distance, we do not mean that technology should make everyone agree with each other. We also do not mean that everyone should feel the same way. A world without disagreement is not only unrealistic. It may not even be desirable.

Science needs disagreement. Business needs different opinions. Politics is naturally a place of competing views. Personal life cannot exist without arguments. Different viewpoints can improve decisions and create new ideas. Generative AI should certainly not act as a judge that decides who is right and who is wrong. What should be reduced are unnecessary gaps in understanding. In other words, AI should help people recognize that one sentence may have different meanings. It should identify missing background information. It should separate “what the other person actually said” from “what I think the other person was suggesting.” It should preserve real uncertainty. It should also help both sides understand why they disagree, even if the disagreement remains.

Success should not be measured by whether everyone finally agrees. It should be measured by whether both sides truly understand where their disagreement actually lies.

For generative AI, this suggests a different path of development.

First, success should not be measured only by speed, volume, and efficiency. It should also be measured by the quality of understanding. Generative AI can help people communicate faster. But if misunderstanding also increases at the same time, then being “faster” does not mean very much.

Second, generative AI should not become an authority that decides the “correct way to think” or the “correct way to speak.”  Generative AI can help people understand how their words may be interpreted by others. But it should not remove reasonable differences in expression simply to create surface-level harmony.

Third, AI should be an objective companion rather than the final judge. Its role should be to encourage reflection and broaden the user’s view, rather than deciding what the user should believe.

Finally, humans should continue to take an active role in important communication. Choosing a word, asking a question, explaining an idea, or taking responsibility for something that has been said may seem troublesome. But these processes are themselves part of understanding.

A different definition of “progress”

The history of communication technology is, in many ways, a history of reducing distance.

The telegraph separated information from the speed of physical travel. The telephone allowed voices to cross distance. Computer networks connected machines and institutions. The Web connected information on a global scale. Mobile and social technologies made communication increasingly immediate and continuous.

Each development made the world physically smaller.

Generative AI introduces a different opportunity because it does not only transport human communication. It can participate in creating and interpreting it.

This makes the next challenge more difficult, but also more important.

If generative AI develops without considering the distance between human understandings, it may automate the problems that already exist. It may allow us to produce misunderstandings faster, defend incomplete interpretations more persuasively, confirm our existing views more comfortably, and distribute poorly aligned messages at unprecedented scale.

We may become more connected while becoming less understood.

items.title: Nvidia Chief Seen As Target of Chinese Spy Plot
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from The New York Times: American spy agencies had gathered striking intelligence. A top executive at a Singapore-based data center company was under scrutiny for possibly steering advanced Nvidia A.I. chips to China. And now American officials had concluded that she was a Chinese intelligence asset (source paywalled; alternative source), funneling information to Beijing. But what came next was even more alarming. Surveillance of the executive, Alice Huang or Huang Le, a Chinese citizen, revealed that she had developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang, Nvidia's chief executive.
 
For years, Washington has worked to deny China the technology needed to match or surpass the United States in the intense global competition for superiority in artificial intelligence. The discovery that Beijing was getting reports from someone with direct access to Mr. Huang, one of the most powerful figures in the A.I. revolution as well as an influential ally of President Trump's, set off alarms at the White House. Roughly a year ago, Mr. Trump was briefed about the intelligence findings, which have not been previously reported, and chose not to do anything with the information. Mr. Trump has been wary of disrupting Nvidia's chip sales, which are helping to drive the economy and the stock market, and of further complicating the trading relationship with China.
 
This account is based on interviews with people briefed on the surveillance, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because the findings are drawn from classified intelligence, as well as other officials and industry executives and analysts. American officials already suspected that Ms. Huang was helping China evade constraints on its ability to gain access to advanced A.I. chips. But the revelation that she was feeding information directly to Beijing raised more troubling possibilities, including that Mr. Huang had insights into Mr. Trump's thinking on an issue of vital importance to both nations, one likely to come up when the president visits China next month. And it left questions about whether she could be gleaning information about Nvidia, which as much as any company accounts for the lead the United States has maintained in developing cutting-edge A.I. models. The surveillance of Ms. Huang continues, they said, and companies that have been affiliated with her continued this year to purchase Nvidia chips. 

Nvidia said in a statement: "Jensen's interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year." Nvidia is "confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know." Customers like Megaspeed, the company that employed Ms. Huang, "receive ordinary business information -- not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets -- and zero information relevant to national security," the company added.
 
In a statement to The New York Times, Megaspeed said that its "current leadership" takes the matter "extremely seriously and is committed to getting to the facts behind these allegations." It added that "outside counsel has been retained to conduct a thorough internal investigation and has notified the U.S. government that we are fully committed to cooperating."

items.title: Cloud vs. Compliance: Resolving the Tug of War over Data Residency
items.author: Poorvy Sharma
items.content:
It is a Gold Standard for customers to know that their Data is in safe hands, but at the same time promise of cloud computing was internet without borders, frictionless, global channel where data flowed seamlessly. This article is based on the experience with working for Cloud Platforms that provide services around the globe. The article focuses to explain that when clients sign the Standard Contractual Clauses with the cloud platform providers, it does not automatically guarantee the data will not cross borders even when the data is stored locally in their region. This is because the Cloud Platforms are dynamic in nature as they take automated backups, integrate with other systems to automate processes. To ensure data privacy it is necessary to use hardware security solutions in the server to ensure no data leaks as well as no entry from back door to the servers. There have been many cases reported for cross border data transfers.

For Technical Architects of a Cloud platform, Data safeguarding is one of the key challenges of their day-to-day work. With the increase in the number of cases of identity thefts, every region’s government has to implement regulatory framework to safeguard their citizen’s data.

It is very important to understand the difference between Data residency and genuine digital sovereignty. While Data residency is more about the geography where data will be stored or where the castle of data will be built, genuine digital sovereignty speaks more about who has the key to that castle!

Deconstructing the Stack: Residency vs. Sovereignty

Before we analyze how modern architectures adapt, we must first distinctly understand the two terms that are frequently confused as inter related:

It specifies the physical, geographic location where data will be stored or at rest, processed or backed up. Achieving residency is the first challenge of deciding the physical infrastructure as data residency is a geographic constraint. The physical infrastructure challenge is resolved by building or leasing localized data centers. [1, 2, 3]

: In simple terms this is a jurisdictional constraint. It dictates that an organization’s data, metadata, custom code and operational workflows remain governed exclusively by laws of the country data resides in. The data is insulated from foreign extraterritorial access laws (for example the US CLOUD ACT) [1,2,3,4]

Data residency may ensure safety when data is at rest, but what happens to data in transit? This question is answered by understanding the below layers that constitute towards true digital sovereignty, further the pyramid image explains the significance of each layer [a][b][c] :

1.      – The physical location of the data center where data will reside. This makes the base of the pyramid

2.      Access control (Operational Sovereignty): It means administrative and support activities must be done by trust worthy personnel in the country of Data residency

3.      Encryption control (Technical Sovereignty): This means that the client holds the key to the encrypted data and hence the service provider cannot fiddle with something they cannot see!

4.      Legal control of Data (Data Sovereignty): If the software company is headquartered in U.S but stores data in South Africa (that means Data residency is local to South Africa but cloud company is headquartered in U.S) then by lay U.S government can ask provider to hand over the data.

Below are few of the major challenges with achieving Digital sovereignty:

Every innovation is always posed with challenges as detailed and explained in depth in this article [1]

1.      The regulations change by region

2.      Innovations in Technology – We are in the era of AI which changes the equation

3.      Frequently changing Customer expectations – Data privacy is the major concern for all customers

4.      Threats to Data security – Hackers are also becoming creative so it is necessary to upkeep the data protection measures

The market has systematically shifted from centralized public cloud nodes towards highly distributed, isolated and multi-tenant architectures designed for local control. To meet this demand leading global hyperscalers have adopted following engineering strategies [1]:

Is it possible to achieve Data Sovereignty just by signing contracts alone? Simple answer to this question is ‘No’; it has to be enforced using hardware and implementing encryption. Most of the platforms have now deployed the models “bring your own key” and “hold your own key”. These models ensure that the cloud vendor, even if they are compelled by the government to surrender the data, encryption makes it unreadable. All this is good when data is at rest and not in the middle of processing, so how do we protect data when it is being processed? Confidential Computing is the answer to this dilemma. The heart of Confidential Computing is the hardware enclave (CPU chip) also technically called the Trusted Execution Environment, this helps separate the data from cloud and decrypts the data for processing within the enclave, so the cloud service provider still does not see any real data. So, in simple statement is secured using encryption, is safeguarded by network protocols like HTTPS, TLS etc. and then is protected by hardware enclave.

2.      Decoupling and de-risking global infrastructure:

To safeguard data in tough situations like war or disconnection due to hardware or network failures, a local version of the cloud can be created to decouple it from global network. Let us understand it with an example: There is a bank headquartered in New York and has a branch in Spain and Norway. If the bank’s main office in NY suddenly experiences network failure, then its branch in Spain and Norway must still be able to operate and service its customers. Decoupling is how this is achieved.

3.      Balancing global and local partnerships:

Innovation is happening around the globe, so enterprises are inclined to partner up with software providers internationally, but to safeguard data they are also partnering with local providers to stay compliant to local data protection governance.

It is the responsibility of an enterprise to stay compliant with data protection and should not be considered as a company against cloud implementation. With the fast-growing technology and the era of AI, it is imperative that protecting data should be every country’s top priority. Enterprises need to adapt digital infrastructure to stay ahead in the race while protecting the data. The real challenge is to build a cloud strategy in which innovation, data sovereignty, and trust coexist by design. The real world threats call for well defined data governance strategy, a clear understanding of regulatory obligations, and an architecture that incorporates security, privacy and compliance from the outset. In the age of AI, organizations who build responsible innovation on the foundation of data protection will lead the race!

items.title: REPL While It Works: Inspect a Running Python Program Without Pausing It
items.author: David Kra
items.content:
Usually, without interrupting it, you cannot interactively debug, call functions in, or change the values of variables in a running python program. This article’s technique removes the limitation.

There are plenty of python examples showing how an executing script can interrupt its execution to present a console, where you can interact, and then resume execution. Here, the console is your choice of the Python interactive shell prompt, with its Read-Eval-Print Loop (aka REPL), or alternatively, the python PDB debugger.

I wanted to do that interacting, but without the and the parts. While the long running execution continues to run, and without interrupting the program’s flow, I wanted to be able to access objects and invoke other functions concurrently. In the Snow White films, there is a song "Whistle While You Work." (Watch the 1937 version or 2025 version). I wanted to "REPL While It Works."

: The audience for this technique is writers of programs that they use for themselves. Normally, a program’s data and functions, their names, semantics, and usage, are not known by others.

Achieving this objective is not hard. The main features of the solution are:

  1. A convenient repository for pseudo-global objects which can be created, set, and used both by the threads and by you while in the REPL or PDB. Avoid having to use thekeyword.
  2. The application’s real work happens in a started thread or threads.
  3. The main thread, after any initiation and starting the threads, drops into REPL, or PDB, or both, one after the other.

Create a function to hold the pseudoglobal objects as attributes. Add, change, and use them from anywhere. Avoid having to use the keyword.

def g(): # This function is never called. 
    # It just holds attributes which can be added, set and used from anywhere.
    pass
# example attributes
g.d = defaultdict(list)
g.finishedthreads=0
g.startedat=time.time()
  1. The application functions, are (a) first defined, and then (b) some of them are started as threads. These do the application’s work. See the details in the below.
  1. Drop into the interactive REPL ro PDB console, or one after the other.
#This goes at the bottom of the script
while True:	
    # Drop into the PDB console	
    print(f'\n Type os._exit()  to terminate the process abruptly, without flushing file buffers, running finally blocks, or executing atexit cleanups.')	  
    print(f'\n Type sys.exit(0) to terminate the main and daemon threads. It first raises a SystemExit exception in each thread. ')	
    print(" Dropping into the PDB debugger console.")	
    print("	 Type c or continue to leave PDB and continue script execution.")	

    breakpoint()

    # Drop into the REPL console	
    print(" Dropping into the REPL console")	
    print("	 Type <ctrl>D to leave the REPL and continue script execution.")	

    code.interact(local=dict(globals(), **locals()))

. This is the full program, including the features above.

#!/usr/bin/python3
# run multithreaded tasks, with a repl while they run

import code
import time
from collections import defaultdict
import threading 
import os
import sys

# 1 Create the repository

def g(): # This function is never called. It just holds attributes which set and used from anywhere.
	pass
# example attributes
g.threads=[]
g.glock=threading.Lock() #Global lock available to be used by all threads.
g.d = defaultdict(list)
g.finishedthreads=0
g.startedat=time.time()

# 2A Define functions

def aworker(i=1,art=0,ep=1,op=1000):
	wpytid = threading.get_ident()
	wostid=  threading.get_native_id()
	wname = threading.current_thread().name
	g.d[i]={"i":i, "name":wname, "wpytid":wpytid, "wostid": wostid}
	print("Thread started: ",g.d[i])
	print(f"Parms = {i=}, {art=}, {ep=}, {op=}") 
	time.sleep(5)
	
	# Resource Lock aquire and use
	#   defined elsewhere: g.glock=threading.Lock()
	g.glock.acquire()
	try: # This try - finally avoids deadlocks if what is inside throws an exception
		print("Acquired ", g.glock)
		whatever=0
	finally:
		g.glock.release()  

	time.sleep(50)
	g.finishedthreads+=1
    g.d[i]["Terminated"]=True
	print(f'Thread terminating {wname}')



def analyze():
		pass

def periodicresultssofar():
	# started as a thread
	while True:
		time.sleep(600)
		analyze()
		if g.finishedthreads==g.qthreads: return

# 2b Launch threads	

qthreads=12
g.qthreads=qthreads
for t in range(1,qthreads+1):
	w = threading.Thread(name=f'Worker-{t}',target=aworker, args=([t]), kwargs={"ep":1,"op": 3}, daemon=True)

 
	g.threads.append(w)
	w.start()
	print(f"Thread Name: {w.name}")
	print(f"Python Thread ID (.ident): {w.ident}")
	print(f"OS Native Thread ID (.native_id): {w.native_id}")

# periodic results so far

p=threading.Thread(name=f'PeriodicResultsSoFar',target=periodicresultssofar, daemon=True)
p.start()
g.threads.append(p)
print(f"Thread Name: {p.name}")
print(f"Python Thread ID (.ident): {p.ident}")
print(f"OS Native Thread ID (.native_id): {p.native_id}")

# 3 Repeatedly drop into the PDB and then the REPL console.

while True:
	# Drop into the PDB console
	print(" Dropping into the PDB console.")
	print(f'\n Type os._exit()  to terminate the process abruptly, without flushing file buffers, running finally blocks, or executing atexit cleanups.')
	print(f'\n Type sys.exit(0) to terminate the main thread and daemon threads. It first raises a SystemExit exception. ')
	print("	Type c or continue to exit the debugger and let the script continue.")
	print("	Type analyze()  to analyze what has been processed so far")
	breakpoint() 

	# Drop into the REPL console
	print(" Dropping into the REPL console")
	print("	Type <ctrl>D to exit the REPL and let the script continue.")
	code.interact(local=dict(globals(), **locals()))

How did I use this? I created a multithreaded program which accesses my gmail account. The threads divided up the work of collecting the sender and size of each of the account’s 100K emails. With gmail’s IMAP response time of about 3 seconds per request, it took many hours. This technique let me run my analyze function whenever I wanted even while the data was still being collected. This let me satisfy my curiosity to find the top senders, so far, in terms of total bytes in all the emails for that sender.

Singapore, Singapore, October 29th, 2026/Chainwire/--, the Binance-backed crypto travel booking platform, today announced AVA+ Partners, a new program that will provide crypto projects with a route to having their token accepted as a payment method on Travala by buying and locking AVA, the token at the heart of the Travala ecosystem.

The program, which is currently in development, will require partner projects to hold AVA for as long as their token is accepted on Travala while receiving partner rewards throughout the partnership.

AVA+ Partners involves three steps for crypto partner projects:

  1. Buy AVA. Partner projects acquire AVA on the open market.
  2. Buy NFT. Partner projects acquire a Travel Tiger NFT.
  3. Activate & Lock. Partner projects activate a Smart Diamond membership and lock AVA in a dedicated AVA+ Partners smart contract for as long as the project’s token is accepted on Travala.

Projects can withdraw from AVA+ Partners at any time. Those that leave the program early contribute part of their locked AVA to the , which Travala has committed never to sell or transfer from. All partner projects are subject to Travala’s approval.

“AVA+ Partners turns real-world utility on Travala into a long-term commitment to AVA,” said Steve Hipwell, AVA Foundation Lead Contributor. “It’s a use case that grows directly with the expansion of our partner and payment ecosystem.”

The initiative is the latest in a string of joint Travala and AVA ecosystem announcements. AVA locked in AVA+ Partners builds towards the long-term goal of achieving 30% of AVA’s circulating supply locked, with AVA locked by partner projects counted alongside AVA locked through the AVA Smart Program and AVA+ Rewards. Full terms, including withdrawal fees, will be set out in each partner agreement.

AVA+ Partners is offered to approved business partners only, under individual agreements, and may be modified or discontinued. This announcement is for information only; it is not an offer, solicitation or inducement to acquire, hold or lock AVA, and is not directed at persons in the United Kingdom, the United Arab Emirates or any jurisdiction where distribution would be unlawful. References to Travala are to TravelFront and its group companies.

Founded in 2017 and now backed by industry giant Binance, Travala is the leading crypto-native travel booking service, offering 2,200,000+ properties across 230 countries, 600+ airlines, 50,000+ car rental locations, and 400,000+ activities globally.
