items.title: Poetry vs uv: Choosing a Python Package Manager
items.author: Michael
items.content:
Poetry and uv are both Python package managers built to solve the same problem, which is making sure every machine installs exactly the same dependencies. Here’s how the two compare on speed, lockfiles, and day-to-day workflow, and why I now point teams to uv.

On a Monday morning, Ada clones a Python project, runs the install command, and the tests pass. On Thursday, Sam clones the exact same commit, runs the exact same command, and three tests fail.

Nobody changed a line of code between Monday and Thursday. What changed was the outside world, as somewhere in the project’s dependency tree, unknowingly, a library the project uses had shipped a new minor version on Wednesday night. Ada got the old one while Sam got the new one. The project said “any version above 2.0 is fine”, and both of them were technically right.

Every Python developer, to be honest, every developer has lived some version of this. It’s the reason “” is a joke that never stops being funny, and it’s the problem Python package managers like Poetry and uv were built to kill.

Recently, I approved a pull request on an open-source Python project I help co-maintain. This PR moved the whole project, all 111 locked dependency versions of it, from Poetry to uv, spanning the local development, CI, release publishing, and the Docker image. The thing I praised in my review wasn’t the speed, although the speed is real; it was a single flag, which was used everywhere. By the end of this piece, you’ll know why that flag matters more than any benchmark.

But first, the problem both tools are solving.

Think of your project’s dependencies as a recipe.

A recipe says “two cups of flour, one stick of butter and a pinch of salt”; it doesn’t say which brand of flour, which batch, or which store to get it from. That’s fine for a recipe; it’s meant to be flexible, and in Python that flexible recipe lives in :

[project]
dependencies = [
    "httpx>=0.27",
    "pydantic>=2.0",
]

means “any version from 0.27 upward”. Today that resolves to one version; next month it might resolve to another and itself depends on other packages which depend on others, each with its own flexible range.

A receipt is different; it says exactly what you bought, it tells you the brand, the size, the batch number and the timestamp of when you paid. If you hand the receipt to someone else, they can buy exactly the same things.

That receipt is a , it records the precise version of every package in the tree, direct and indirect, plus a hash of each file so nobody can quietly swap one out. Ada and Sam’s problem was that their project had a recipe and no receipt; each of them shopped on a different day and came home with a different brand and batch of flour bought from different stores.

Poetry and uv both give you a receipt; they just take very different amounts of time to write it, and they disagree on one important question: what should happen when the recipe and the receipt stop matching?

Poetry: The One That Fixed It First.

Poetry arrived in 2018, at a time when Python packaging was a pile of separate tools glued together with habit. You used to install things, to isolate them, to pin them, and file to package them, and to upload them. Every project did it slightly differently.

Poetry put all of that behind one command line and one file; now you declared dependencies in , it resolved them, wrote a receipt, created a virtual environment for you, and could build and publish your package when you were ready.

poetry new myapp      # scaffold a package
poetry add httpx      # add a dependency and update the lockfile
poetry install        # install everything from poetry.lock
poetry run pytest     # run a command inside the environment
poetry build          # build a wheel and source distribution
poetry publish        # upload to PyPI

For a lot of teams, including the project I mentioned earlier, Poetry was the first time Python dependency management felt calm. It deserves real credit for that; it made lockfiles normal in Python and treated publishing a library as a first-class job instead of an afterthought.

It also has costs you start to feel as a project grows.

Poetry is written in Python, and its dependency resolver works carefully through version constraints. On a small project you would barely notice this, but on a project with a deep tree, resolving and installing can take long enough that you go and make a cup of coffee.

It’s one tool among several. Poetry manages your project’s dependencies, but it doesn’t install Python itself. You still need something like to get the right interpreter, and something like to install command-line tools globally. The patchwork got smaller, not gone.

Its config was its own dialect for years. Until version 2.0, which was released in early 2025, Poetry kept project metadata under its own section instead of the standard table every other tool reads. Version 2.0 adopted the standard, which helps, but many older projects still carry the old format.

None of these are dealbreakers; they’re the kind of friction you stop noticing until something removes it.

uv: Same Job, Different Engine

uv first appeared in February 2024. It's a Python package manager written in Rust, and it started life as a much faster . It didn't stay that small for long.

Today, one uv binary covers what used to take five or six tools:

uv python install 3.12          # install a Python interpreter (replaces pyenv)
uv init myapp                   # start a project
uv add httpx                    # add a dependency and update uv.lock
uv add --dev pytest             # add a development-only dependency
uv sync                         # make the environment match the lockfile
uv run pytest                   # run inside the environment
uvx ruff check .                # run a CLI tool without installing it (replaces pipx)
uv build                        # build a wheel and source distribution
uv publish                      # upload to PyPI

If you've read older comparisons that say uv can't publish packages, that was true in its early months. It isn't anymore. and both exist, and uv now ships its own build backend, . The project I reviewed switched to it as part of the migration.

The commands look almost the same as Poetry's, but most importantly, the experience doesn't.

uv vs Poetry: The Speed Is Not an Exaggeration

Rather than quote someone else's numbers, I ran my own. Same machine, same Python 3.12, the same nine dependencies (, , , , , , , , ), with every cache wiped before each round. Three rounds each, median shown:

                                   Poetry     uv
Fresh add, empty cache             22.2s      4.0s
Reinstall into a new venv          2.8s       0.11s

Both tools installed the same set of packages. The cold run is about five times faster, while the warm reinstall, which is what happens every time someone recreates a virtual environment or CI restores a cache, is roughly 25 times faster. It finishes so quickly the first time that you'll probably check whether it actually did anything.

Your numbers will differ with your network, disk, and dependency tree, so run the comparison on your own project, but the gap is consistently large, not marginal.

Two things do most of the work.

The first is the obvious one: the resolver and installer are compiled code, and they download and unpack packages in parallel.

The second matters more day to day. uv keeps one global cache of every package it has ever downloaded, and when it builds a virtual environment, it links files out of that cache instead of copying them. A new environment for a package you've used before is mostly a matter of creating links, which is close to free. Ten projects that all use share one copy on disk instead of ten.

Speed isn't really the point.

Here's the part most comparisons skip. The headline is "uv is fast," but the bigger change is that you stop thinking about the machinery.

With uv, you never have to create a virtual environment, name it, activate it, or remember to deactivate it. notices the project, checks that the environment matches the lockfile, fixes it if needed, and runs your command. You can clone a uv project and type as your very first command, and it will install Python if needed, build the environment, and run the tests.

It also handles single files. You can put a script's dependencies at the top of the script itself:

# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.12"
# dependencies = ["httpx"]
# ///
import httpx
print(httpx.get("https://example.com").status_code)

Run it with , and uv builds a throwaway environment with in it. No project, no , no "which venv was this for again?" uv add --script fetch.py httpx writes that header block for you. If you share small tools with teammates, this alone is worth the switch.

Since so much of uv's speed comes from the cache, it helps to know how to control it.

uv cache clean            # wipe the whole cache
uv cache clean httpx      # remove just one package from the cache
uv sync --refresh         # re-check package indexes online instead of trusting cached metadata
uv run --no-cache ...     # ignore the cache completely for this one run

The difference between the last two is worth getting right. still uses the cache, but it asks the package index again whether anything new has been published, which is what you want when you know a fix was just released. doesn't read from or write to your cache at all. It uses a temporary directory for that one command, which is useful when you suspect a corrupted download and want to prove it.

and tell you how much space it's using and where. On a busy laptop, the answer is often "more than you'd guess," and clears out entries nothing uses anymore.

: The Flag I Praised

Now back to Ada and Sam, and to that pull request.

uv is built to be convenient, and part of that convenience is that it keeps the receipt up to date for you. If you edit by hand and then run or , uv notices the recipe changed, quietly re-resolves, rewrites , and carries on.

On your own laptop, that's exactly what you want.

In CI, or in a Docker build, or in a release pipeline, it's a trap. Imagine someone changes a version range in and forgets to commit the updated . A convenient tool fixes it silently in the CI machine's working copy, the build goes green, and the receipt in your repository is now wrong. Nobody notices until someone else's machine resolves something different. That's Ada and Sam all over again, except now you have a lockfile, so everyone believes the problem is impossible.

turns that silent fix into a loud failure:

It installs strictly from the existing , and if the is out of date with , it refuses and exits with an error. I tested this by changing a project's dependencies without relocking:

$ uv sync --locked
error: The lockfile at `uv.lock` needs to be updated, but `--locked` was provided.

hint: To update the lockfile, run `uv lock`.

Exit code 1. The build stops, and the person who forgot to commit the lockfile finds out in minutes instead of weeks.

There are three modes worth keeping straight:

uv sync            update the lockfile if needed, then install       (local development)
uv sync --locked   fail if the lockfile is out of date, then install (CI, Docker, releases)
uv sync --frozen   install from the lockfile without checking it     (when you trust it completely)

does the check on its own without installing anything, which makes a cheap first step in a CI job or a pre-commit hook.

That's what I liked about the migration. Every place that installs dependencies in an automated setting- the Makefile targets, the CI workflows, and the Docker build- used . Outdated lockfiles fail out loud instead of being patched up quietly. The tool's convenience stays on developers' laptops, where it belongs, and strictness takes over everywhere else.

To be fair to Poetry, it also refuses to install when is badly out of sync with , and does the same job as . The difference is the default. uv leans towards fixing things for you, so you have to choose strictness explicitly. That's not a flaw, as long as you know it's a choice you need to make.

When Poetry Still Makes Sense

I'm going to point you towards uv, but there are honest reasons to wait.

If your project is stable, your team knows Poetry well, installs are fast enough, and nothing hurts, there's no prize for migrating this week. A working toolchain is worth a lot.

If you lean on Poetry plugins, for things like dynamic versioning from git tags or exporting in a particular format, check that each one has a uv equivalent before you start. Some do, some need a small script, and some don't yet.

And if your release process is deeply tied to and Poetry's publishing flow, budget time to rebuild it rather than assuming it will just carry over.

None of these are reasons to stay forever. They're reasons to plan the switch instead of doing it on a Friday afternoon.

How to Migrate From Poetry to uv

For most projects, migration is a short afternoon, not a project. The same 111 dependencies came across in the PR I reviewed, with every locked version preserved.

There's a community tool that does most of the conversion:

It rewrites sections into the standard table, moves development dependencies into , and generates using your existing as a constraint, so you get the same versions you already had instead of whatever's newest today. I ran it on a test project, and it finished in about a second.

After that, the work is mostly find-and-replace across the places that call Poetry:

poetry install           ->  uv sync --locked
poetry run <cmd>         ->  uv run <cmd>
poetry add <pkg>         ->  uv add <pkg>
poetry add -G dev <pkg>  ->  uv add --dev <pkg>
poetry lock              ->  uv lock
poetry build             ->  uv build
poetry publish           ->  uv publish

Then check the places people forget:

  • Swap the Poetry setup step for uv's, point dependency caching at , and use on every install.
  • Copy the uv binary in, run uv sync --locked --no-dev for production images, and make sure the container starts through the environment's Python rather than a wrapper that no longer exists.
  • Anything that shells out to .
  • , if anyone still needs one. uv export --format requirements-txt generates it from the lockfile, so it never drifts.
  • The README's "getting started" section is the first thing a new contributor runs.

Finally, run your full test suite on a clean machine, not just your laptop with its warm caches. Build the wheel, install it fresh, and make sure your command-line entry points still work. The PR I reviewed did exactly that, and the Docker image got its own manual check, because the existing compatibility tests only covered older images and wouldn't have caught a broken build.

Back to Monday and Thursday

Go back to Ada and Sam one last time.

Their problem was never really about which tool they used. It was that their project had a recipe and no reliable receipt, and nothing stopped the two from drifting apart. Poetry solved that years ago, and it deserves the credit. uv solves the same problem, then removes most of the waiting and most of the separate tools around it: Python installs, virtual environments, global CLI tools, and one-off scripts.

If I had to sum it up for a team choosing today, it would be this. Start new projects with uv, move existing ones when you next have a quiet week, and wherever a machine installs your dependencies without a human watching, add , so the day your recipe and receipt disagree, you hear about it immediately instead of three tests and three days later.

items.title: Canada to Join EU Network of Supercomputers
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Canada is joining the European Union's supercomputing network to give Canadian companies, startups, and researchers access to European computing resources for AI development. The partnership aims to strengthen AI cooperation and reduce dependence on US technology. Politico reports: The EU's supercomputing network is run by the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking, an EU public-private vehicle with an 8.2 billion-euro budget. The network consists of 14 supercomputers (some ranked in the global top 10), 19 AI-focused AI factories and 10 quantum computers. The vehicle will also run seven massive AI data center hubs, known as AI gigafactories, set to be built next year with a total investment cost of 30 billion euros.
 
Experts praised a possible EU-Canadian compute power team-up, but warned it's only the start. "Compute cooperation is one of the most obvious short-term 'middle power' cooperation plays in AI," said Anton Leicht, technology and international affairs fellow at Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. But he added that for now "it doesn't put a dent into the actual dependence" on the U.S. "As long as the U.S. builds gigawatt-scale clusters, no amount of cooperation that doesn't result in massive buildouts will help," he said.
 
Canada's engagement in the EU's supercomputer network builds further on Canada's previous partial involvement in the EU's flagship research and development program, Horizon Europe. Horizon Europe partially funds EuroHPC. To date, 38 countries have participated in the EU's supercomputing network: 27 EU member countries plus non-EU countries including Norway, Switzerland, the United Kingdom, Israel and Turkey.

items.title: Frgmnt CEO Aurélien Roussel on How Finance Teams Can Earn Yield on Stablecoins Onchain
items.author: Ishan Pandey
items.content:
Stablecoins have grown to $301.4 billion in DefiLlama's snapshot of 20 October 2026, yet the dollars that a business holds in them earn no lending yield until someone compares lending markets, checks collateral and withdrawal liquidity and arranges custody, which are tasks that sit well outside the usual work of a finance team.

Frgmnt is a stablecoin protocol on Base that curates non-custodial Morpho Vault strategies for institutions while its Founding Allocator Program gives an initial cohort of 10 institutional allocators access to those strategies with onboarding through Anchorage Digital, dedicated reporting and regular strategy reviews. Today we sit down with Aurélien Roussel, co-founder and CEO of Frgmnt and former chief operating officer of Bricks.co, to discuss how a finance team decides which part of its treasury belongs onchain, how Frgmnt chooses the lending opportunities behind its strategies and what he hopes to learn from the first ten institutions.

Hi Aurélien, welcome to our "Behind the Startup" series. You moved from helping scale Bricks.co to founding Frgmnt. Take us through that journey. What drew you toward stablecoins and how did you decide it was time to build something of your own?

My experience at Bricks.co taught me how to build and scale a financial product around a simple idea: making investment opportunities more accessible to a much broader audience. It also showed me that technology alone is not enough. You need a product people understand, a reliable operating model, and above all, trust.

When I started looking more closely at digital assets, stablecoins stood out to me. They had already become an important part of the financial system, but much of that capital was still sitting idle or earning yield through fragmented, complex DeFi strategies.

I saw an opportunity to bring those worlds closer together: the simplicity and utility of stablecoins with the efficiency of onchain finance. Frgmnt came from that conviction. I wanted to build something of our own that could make this infrastructure genuinely useful, first for individual users and increasingly for businesses and institutions.

Why did you choose to build Frgmnt around making stablecoin capital productive? Was there a particular experience or conversation that made the opportunity clear to you and how did you decide what to build first?

It was less one particular conversation than a recurring observation: people were adopting stablecoins as a way to hold and transfer dollars digitally, but making those dollars productive often required them to understand multiple protocols, compare rates, manage liquidity, and take responsibility for operational complexity.

That creates a gap between what the technology can do and what most users are comfortable doing themselves. For a business, the challenge is even greater because capital allocation also involves internal controls, reporting, and risk management.

We decided to start with the core problem: how to allocate stablecoin capital across selected onchain lending strategies without forcing users to manage every underlying position themselves. Frgmnt combines stablecoin infrastructure with a strategy allocation layer designed to assess opportunities and manage allocations as conditions change.

The principle is simple: users should not need to become DeFi specialists to access onchain financial infrastructure. Our job is to make that infrastructure easier to use, easier to monitor, and more relevant to real financial needs.

A finance team might need to make payments tomorrow while holding other funds for several months. Where does Frgmnt fit into that picture and how would the team use it in practice?

The starting point is to recognize that not all treasury capital has the same purpose or time horizon. A company needs immediate liquidity for payroll, suppliers, and operating expenses. Other funds may not be needed for weeks or months.

We do not believe all of that money should be treated in the same way. Funds required for immediate payments should remain in appropriate liquid arrangements. For a portion of its treasury that the company can allocate to onchain strategies, Frgmnt can provide access to selected lending opportunities through a more structured interface.

In practice, the finance team would assess its liquidity requirements, define the amount it is prepared to allocate, and select a strategy consistent with its risk constraints and investment horizon. The team would then use reporting and ongoing monitoring to follow its positions.

The objective is not to replace a company's bank or compromise its ability to make payments. It is to give finance teams another way to manage eligible digital-dollar balances while remaining conscious of liquidity, operational, and smart-contract risks.

You have just launched the Founding Allocator Program, initially limited to 10 institutions. Why did you choose to start with a small group and what do you hope to learn by working with the first pilot participants?

We deliberately chose a small initial group because institutional adoption requires more than a functioning smart contract. It requires confidence in the process around the product: onboarding, strategy selection, reporting, operational procedures, and communication when market conditions change.

Working with ten initial allocators allows us to build those processes closely with the people who will actually use them. We want to understand how their teams evaluate onchain opportunities, what information they need before allocating capital, how they define acceptable liquidity constraints, and what their internal approval processes look like.

The program gives participants access to curated Morpho Vault strategies, with dedicated reporting and regular strategy reviews. In return, their feedback helps us improve both the product and the institutional experience around it.

We see this as a foundation for long-term distribution, rather than simply a short-term acquisition campaign. If we can demonstrate that onchain strategies can be accessed through a disciplined and transparent process, we can build a much stronger basis for broader institutional adoption.

The program includes dedicated reporting, regular strategy reviews and direct access to your team. What will that working relationship look like for an allocator and how will you help its finance team get comfortable with using onchain lending?

We want the relationship to feel like a working partnership, not simply access to a vault address. Institutions need to understand what they are allocating to, why a strategy has been selected, and what could change its risk profile.

That is why we combine access to selected Morpho Vault strategies with dedicated reporting, regular strategy reviews, and direct communication with our team. The aim is to explain the underlying markets, allocation rationale, liquidity conditions, and the risks that come with onchain lending in language that a finance team can evaluate.

Onboarding is also important. Where relevant, we work with partners such as Anchorage to support the institutional access process and help align the setup with each participant's requirements.

We do not expect trust to come from a presentation or a headline yield figure. It comes from making the strategy understandable, being transparent about its limitations, and maintaining consistent communication. Our role is to help institutions make informed decisions, not to suggest that onchain lending is risk-free.

The Founding Allocator Program extends that route to curated Morpho Vault strategies. Frgmnt states that participants pay no program fees, face no lock-up and can withdraw on the same day under normal operating conditions, with allocations and underlying activity open to review through onchain data as well as dedicated reporting.

The program gives participants access to Morpho Vault strategies curated by Frgmnt. How do you choose the lending opportunities behind those strategies and how do you balance the returns participants are looking for with the liquidity they need?

We do not look at yield in isolation. A high advertised rate is only useful if the underlying opportunity is compatible with the allocator's risk profile and liquidity requirements.

Our assessment considers several factors: the quality and concentration of collateral, market utilization, borrower demand, liquidity available for withdrawals, smart-contract and oracle risks, and the characteristics of the underlying lending markets. We also look at how quickly conditions can change and whether a strategy remains appropriate under less favorable market scenarios.

From there, allocation is about balancing competing objectives. A strategy designed for capital that may be needed soon should not necessarily look like one designed for a longer investment horizon. We aim to select and adjust allocations based on both the expected return and the risks required to pursue it.

Morpho provides the vault infrastructure, while our curation and allocation approach focuses on selecting suitable opportunities and monitoring their evolution. The goal is not to chase the highest rate at every moment. It is to pursue sustainable, risk-adjusted returns while respecting the constraints that matter to each allocator.

No strategy can eliminate market, liquidity, or protocol risk, and we believe that distinction should remain explicit in every institutional conversation.

How has the move from COO to co-founder and CEO changed the way you spend your time? What part of building Frgmnt has taught you the most about yourself as a founder?

As a COO, I was primarily focused on making the business work: execution, operations, coordination, and turning priorities into concrete results. As a co-founder and CEO, I still care deeply about execution, but I spend much more time deciding what we should not do, where we should focus, and how to build the right relationships for the long term.

At Frgmnt, that means balancing product development with institutional partnerships, distribution, risk management, fundraising, and team building. In an emerging market, you cannot simply copy a proven playbook. You have to keep learning while making decisions with incomplete information.

The biggest lesson for me has been the importance of focus and credibility. It is tempting to pursue every opportunity in a market as dynamic as DeFi, but a strong business comes from solving a specific problem consistently and earning users' trust over time.

Building Frgmnt has reinforced my belief that ambition and discipline need to go together. We want to build a substantial business, but we need to earn every step of that growth through a product that works and relationships that last.

Last question. If Frgmnt becomes the company you want it to be, how will a finance team’s working day look different? What will it be able to do with its money that it cannot easily do today?

I would like finance teams to spend less time navigating fragmented infrastructure and more time making decisions about their capital.

Today, accessing onchain opportunities can mean evaluating multiple protocols, understanding different interfaces, monitoring changing rates, and assembling information from several sources. Those are meaningful barriers for a team whose core responsibility is running a business, not managing DeFi positions.

Our ambition is to make that experience much more integrated. A finance team should be able to identify which portion of its stablecoin balances is suitable for deployment, understand the strategy and its risks, access the relevant infrastructure, and monitor its positions through clear reporting.

Over time, we want Frgmnt to become a bridge between stablecoins and institutional treasury management: combining strategy allocation, onchain infrastructure, and a more familiar operating experience.

Ultimately, making money productive should not require businesses to become experts in every layer of the technology. We want to give them more choice over how they manage digital-dollar liquidity, with the transparency to understand what they are doing and the controls to make decisions responsibly.

Don’t forget to like and share the story!

[...] The transaction is expected to close at the end of 2027 or the first half of 2028. The deal could face scrutiny over its impact on competition, with New York City's Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP) saying on Wednesday that a potential merger continued a "troubling trend" of corporate consolidation. items.title: Building a Docs-as-Code Workflow With Markdown, Mermaid, and GitHub Actions
items.author: Himashi Meththasena
items.content:
Every engineering team starts with noble intentions. A new project launches, and a sleek Notion page or Confluence space is created. Architecture diagrams are drawn, API contracts are detailed, and onboarding guides are carefully written.

The codebase has evolved through dozens of pull requests, hotfixes, and refactors. The documentation, however, remains frozen in time. New developers join the team, follow the setup guide, hit four cryptic setup errors on step two, and realize the docs are a lie.

We’ve all experienced this phenomenon: . Traditional static wikis fail because they live completely detached from where engineers actually spend their time: the code.

Here is how we killed our rotting internal wiki and built a sustainable, auto-updating "Code-First" documentation ecosystem that engineers actually maintain.

The Root Cause: Why Traditional Wikis Fail

Before changing our workflow, we analyzed why our team constantly abandoned Notion and Confluence:

  1. Context Switching Friction: Updating a wiki requires opening a browser tab, finding the right page (out of hundreds of stale ones), and manually syncing code changes. Under deadline pressure, documentation is always the first task dropped.
  2. Zero Quality Control or CI Validation: There is no pull request process for wikis. Code gets tested, reviewed, and block-checked by CI/CD, while documentation lives in an unversioned void where anyone can break accuracy without feedback.
  3. Out-of-Sync Architectural Diagrams: Diagrams drawn in external UI tools become obsolete the moment a microservice endpoint changes or a new message queue is added.

The Solution: The "Code-First Docs" Architecture

We decided to treat documentation as a first-class citizen of our codebase. If code changes, the documentation changes in the exact same Git commit.

Here are the three pillars we implemented to make Docs-as-Code work at scale:

1. Markdown Co-located with Source Code

Instead of centralized external wikis, every repository owns its documentation. High-level architecture, setup guides, and troubleshooting runbooks live inside a directory right next to the source code.

├── .github/
│   └── workflows/
│       └── docs-ci.yml
├── docs/
│   ├── architecture.md
│   ├── onboarding.md
│   └── runbooks/
│       └── high-cpu-troubleshooting.md
├── src/
└── README.md

2. Automated API and Architecture Diagram Generation

We stopped manually drawing architecture diagrams and writing API specs by hand. Instead, we generate them programmatically:

  • We use embedded directly inside Markdown files. When a system flow changes, engineers update simple text definitions rather than dragging shapes in a UI tool.
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    Client->>API Gateway: POST /v1/orders
    API Gateway->>Kafka: Publish OrderCreated Event
    Kafka->>OrderWorker: Consume Event

Moving Beyond Static Annotations

For APIs, we shifted the burden of maintenance entirely to self-documenting code. Rather than manually describing REST endpoints or gRPC contracts in a browser editor, we leveraged code-level annotations, such as OpenAPI and Swagger for REST services, or Protobuf definitions for gRPC. The beauty of this approach is that the API reference documentation generates itself during the build phase. When a developer adds or modifies an endpoint parameter in the codebase, the documentation updates automatically.

Treating Docs Like Code in CI/CD

To guarantee quality, we began reviewing documentation in pull requests right alongside production code. We integrated lightweight documentation validation steps directly into our GitHub Actions pipeline. Automated linters immediately catch broken internal links, dead URLs, or bad formatting before code ever hits .

Once a pull request merges, static site generators like MkDocs Material or Docusaurus automatically pull Markdown files across all our microservices and publish them to a single, beautifully organized, and searchable internal developer portal.

Transitioning from a neglected wiki to a Code-First Docs model fundamentally reshaped our engineering culture.

The most immediate win was in developer onboarding: new engineers went from struggling for two weeks with outdated setup steps to spinning up their local environments in under three days.

Because documentation now lived right next to the code in pull requests, over 85% of architectural PRs began including matching file updates in the exact same commit.

Perhaps best of all, we eliminated lost technical context. Every decision, rationale, and runbook update became fully searchable through and , giving engineers immediate insight into a system was built a certain way without needing to message a senior developer.

Key Takeaways for Engineering Teams

If you want to kill wiki rot in your organization, meet your developers where they already work. Forcing engineers to jump into an external browser portal guarantees documentation will eventually stall and decay.

By pulling docs into the IDE, enforcing freshness through your CI/CD pipeline, and automating diagram generation directly from source code, you transform documentation from an annoying afterthought into a living asset that scales seamlessly with your codebase.

items.title: Building a Client-Side PDF Redaction Engine With PDF.js and pdf-lib
items.author: Elias Miller
items.content:
Every few months, another high-profile document leak hits the headlines. A government agency releases redacted court transcripts, or a corporate legal team publishes "censored" financial filings. Within ten minutes, someone on Reddit or Hacker News drags their cursor across the black bars, hits , pastes it into Notepad, and suddenly, classified names and bank balances appear in plain text.

The culprit is almost always the same: .

Someone took a PDF editor, drew an opaque black annotation rectangle over the text, and exported it. Visually, the sensitive data was hidden. Structurally, the raw text glyphs remained untouched inside the PDF’s content streams.

Even worse? When casual users try to fix this using popular "Free Online PDF Editors," they commit an even greater security cardinal sin: uploading unredacted, confidential documents to an unknown cloud server over the public internet.

In this article, let’s tear down why PDF redaction fails at the binary level, and walk through how we built an irreversible, zero-server document sanitization engine running 100% client-side in the browser.

1. The Anatomy of a PDF Leak

A PDF is not an image; it is an object-oriented document format built on postscript-like streams.

When you see a line of text on a page, the PDF structure looks something like this:

ps
BT
/F1 12 Tf
72 712 Td
(CONFIDENTIAL: User SSN is 000-12-3456) Tj
ET

If an editor merely adds a black rectangle above that text block:

ps
0 0 0 rg
70 710 200 15 re
f

The rendering engine executes sequentially: it paints the text, then draws a black box on top of it. The text stream remains intact. Anyone using a parser (or even a standard browser preview) can still extract the text, run search queries on it, or inspect the document tree.

To truly redact a PDF, you have two choices:

  1. : Parse the content stream, locate character matrices intersecting the bounding box, slice the PostScript operators, and rewrite the font mapping tables. (Extremely fragile; edge cases with kerning, font sub-setting, and vector graphics frequently fail or leave phantom character artifacts).
  2. True Physical Raster Sanitization: Render the target page into an isolated graphics context, physically overwrite the pixel memory with opaque blocks, discard the underlying text objects entirely, and reconstruct the page.

For security-critical applications, Option 2 is mathematically foolproof. If the glyphs no longer exist in the byte array, no parser can ever reconstruct them.

2. The Cloud Privacy Paradox

Before diving into code, let's address the elephant in the room: cloud-based PDF utilities.

When an employee needs to hide trade secrets or medical records, they search for . They upload their sensitive file to a SaaS platform.

  • The user’s goal is .
  • The SaaS model requires uploading over HTTPS to a remote container, storing it in an ephemeral S3 bucket, and processing it on a remote VM.

Even with TLS and "we delete files after 1 hour" promises, you are expanding your attack surface by transmitting raw PII outside your local machine.

The web has evolved. With modern HTML5 Canvas, WebAssembly, and typed arrays, the browser sandbox is more than capable of handling enterprise-grade PDF manipulation with zero bytes leaving the client.

3. Engineering the Engine: Hybrid Sanitization Pipeline

When building our client-side redaction tool, we faced an architectural dilemma:

If you rasterize an entire 200-page document just to redact two words on page 3, you destroy vector crispness for 198 pristine pages and blow up the file size from 2MB to 80MB.

Our solution was a Selective Hybrid Pipeline:

  • : Cloned losslessly as raw vector streams.
  • : Irrevocably burned in-memory via high-DPI canvas buffers.

Here is the architectural workflow:

4. The Code: Irreversible In-Browser Destruction

Let’s look at the core execution pipeline implemented with and .

Step 1: Capturing Normalized Coordinates

The user draws redaction boxes over a responsive preview container. We record coordinates as normalized percentages (0.0 to 1.0) rather than raw screen pixels, ensuring accuracy across any zoom factor or device pixel ratio:

typescript
export interface RedactionBox {
  id: string;
  pageIndex: number; // 0-based
  x: number;         // 0.0 - 1.0
  y: number;         // 0.0 - 1.0
  width: number;     // 0.0 - 1.0
  height: number;    // 0.0 - 1.0
  color: 'black' | 'white';
}

When the user clicks "Export Sanitized Document", we read the binary buffer locally:

typescript
import { PDFDocument } from 'pdf-lib';
async function sanitizePdf(file: File, redactions: RedactionBox[], pdfJsDoc: any): Promise<Blob> {
  const arrayBuffer = await file.arrayBuffer();
  // 1. Load original document strictly in-memory
  const originalPdf = await PDFDocument.load(arrayBuffer, { ignoreEncryption: true });
  const newPdf = await PDFDocument.create();
  const totalPages = originalPdf.getPageCount();
  for (let i = 0; i < totalPages; i++) {
    const pageBoxes = redactions.filter((b) => b.pageIndex === i);
    if (pageBoxes.length === 0) {
      // BRANCH A: Clean page -> Lossless vector clone
      const [copiedPage] = await newPdf.copyPages(originalPdf, [i]);
      newPdf.addPage(copiedPage);
    } else {
      // BRANCH B: Dirty page -> Physical pixel wipeout
      const pdfPage = await pdfJsDoc.getPage(i + 1);
      
      // 2.0x scale guarantees ~200 DPI crisp print quality
      const scale = 2.0;
      const viewport = pdfPage.getViewport({ scale });
      const canvas = document.createElement('canvas');
      canvas.width = Math.floor(viewport.width);
      canvas.height = Math.floor(viewport.height);
      const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d')!;
      // Render base document into canvas
      ctx.fillStyle = '#ffffff';
      ctx.fillRect(0, 0, canvas.width, canvas.height);
      await pdfPage.render({ canvasContext: ctx, viewport }).promise;
      // Physically burn opaque pixels directly into the canvas buffer!
      pageBoxes.forEach((box) => {
        const rx = Math.round(box.x * viewport.width);
        const ry = Math.round(box.y * viewport.height);
        const rw = Math.round(box.width * viewport.width);
        const rh = Math.round(box.height * viewport.height);
        ctx.fillStyle = box.color === 'white' ? '#ffffff' : '#000000';
        ctx.fillRect(rx, ry, rw, rh);
      });
      // Convert sanitized canvas back to binary image stream
      const sanitizedBlob = await new Promise<Blob | null>((res) =>
        canvas.toBlob(res, 'image/jpeg', 0.94)
      );
      if (!sanitizedBlob) throw new Error('Rasterization failure');
      const imgBytes = await sanitizedBlob.arrayBuffer();
      const embeddedImg = await newPdf.embedJpg(imgBytes);
      // Re-create the page preserving original physical dimensions
      const originalPage = originalPdf.getPage(i);
      const { width, height } = originalPage.getSize();
      const newPage = newPdf.addPage([width, height]);
      newPage.drawImage(embeddedImg, {
        x: 0,
        y: 0,
        width,
        height,
      });
    }
  }
  // 3. Serialize and return local blob URL
  const finalPdfBytes = await newPdf.save();
  return new Blob([finalPdfBytes], { type: 'application/pdf' });
}

Executing high-resolution rasterization in a browser tab comes with pitfalls:

  1. Garbage Collection Pressure:
  2. Large PDFs can generate hundreds of megabytes of raw image data during processing.
  • Never retain canvas instances in global variables.
  • Set canvas.width = 0; canvas.height = 0; after converting to blob to free memory immediately.
  • Always call URL.revokeObjectURL(prevUrl) when regenerating downloads.
  1. Touch & Pan Frictionless UX:
  2. Users redact on laptops, iPads, and trackpads. Implementing an overlay that distinguishes between and requires a drag threshold:
typescript
const DRAG_THRESHOLD = 8; // Screen pixels
if (screenDistance < DRAG_THRESHOLD) {
  // Treat as tap or gesture, do not draw accidental mini-boxes
  return;
}

6. The Verdict: Local-First is the Real Future of Utility Software

For years, developers were trained to default to the cloud:

"Need to convert a PDF? Spin up an AWS Lambda with Poppler."

"Need to redact an invoice? Send it to our REST endpoint."

This architecture was never about user convenience; it was driven by legacy browser limitations and SaaS monetization models.

Today, with the power of modern client-side engines:

  • : Deployable for $0 on Cloudflare Pages or GitHub Pages.
  • True zero-knowledge privacy: Your sensitive tax files or medical records never leave your RAM.
  • Zero data liability for builders: You cannot leak user data if you never store it in the first place.

If you are manipulating user files in 2026, ask yourself: Does this data really need to touch your cloud backend? Chances are, the user's browser is already more than fast enough to do it itself.

items.title: Distributed Locks Are More Dangerous Than They Look
items.author: Jaswanth Mopathi
items.content:
A distributed lock is not a bigger mutex

A distributed lock is not a bigger mutex. It is a different animal wearing the same costume, and the costume is what gets people hurt.

Distributed locks look deceptively similar to local mutexes. You acquire, you perform a critical operation, you release. That resemblance is dangerous.

A local mutex lives inside one failure domain. A distributed lock spans processes and networks and clocks and storage, along with failure detectors that can disagree with each other. The lock service may correctly decide that ownership changed while the previous holder is still running or paused or partitioned, or while it is quietly carrying delayed requests.

The central question is whether an obsolete client can still produce effects after its authority has ended. Martin Kleppmann frames the same divide as locks used for efficiency versus locks used for correctness. In the correctness case duplicate execution becomes corruption rather than wasted work.

A lock is not a critical section

Consider a lease-backed lock around a reconciliation job.

Lease lease = lockService.acquire("order:" + orderId, Duration.ofSeconds(15));

try {
    reconcile(orderId);
} finally {
    lockService.release(lease);
}

The code is locally reasonable and globally unsafe. Suppose the process pauses for 30 seconds after acquisition. Maybe garbage collection stalls it, maybe the CPU is starved, maybe it is paging, maybe something sends it a stop signal. The lease expires, another worker acquires the lock, and the original process later resumes. Nothing in the resumed process proves that authority still exists.

A delayed network request creates the same failure even when the process never pauses at all. Checking the lease immediately before a write does not close the race, because execution can pause in the gap between the check and the write. Kleppmann uses this stale holder problem to show why even a perfect lock service does not automatically make protected resource access safe.

Coordination systems can provide strong ownership semantics without controlling the resource that actually matters. The ZooKeeper lock recipe uses ephemeral sequential znodes and gives the lock to the client with the lowest sequence number. etcd ties lock ownership to a lease and releases the lock when that lease expires. Those mechanisms establish authority inside the coordinator. They do nothing to stop an old process from writing to an external resource after ownership has changed.

Leases trade deadlock for stale ownership

Leases exist because permanent locks have a severe liveness problem. A crashed owner can block progress forever. Time-bounded authority lets another participant proceed after expiration, but now time becomes part of the safety argument.

Redis Redlock computes a remaining validity window from the elapsed acquisition time and assumes local clocks progress at roughly the same rate with bounded drift relative to the TTL. Current Redis documentation also warns that TTL expiration does not use a monotonic clock, and that a shift in the wall clock can compromise consistency.

Lease expiration is not necessarily a single instant that everyone observes at once. Consul documents TTL as a lower bound for invalidation. Expiration will not occur before the TTL, but it may occur later. Consul warns about clock skew too. More fundamentally, it notes that failure detection can produce false positives and release a lock while the owner is still alive. Disabling those checks improves safety at the expense of liveness. Faster failure detection improves progress but raises the risk of overlapping authority.

Lease renewal reduces probability, not category. Extending a TTL helps a long-running operation, but it cannot make networks timely, or process pauses bounded. Redis documentation now states that lock retention must not be assumed merely because the owning process is still alive, and it recommends fencing tokens for work that runs long.

Fencing moves safety to the resource

A fencing token is a monotonically increasing value issued whenever ownership changes. Every protected operation carries that token. The resource remembers the highest token it has accepted and rejects any request carrying an older value. This converts a timing problem into an ordering problem. A stale process may resume, and an old RPC may arrive late, but neither one can overwrite state once a newer owner has advanced the fence.

The essential logic belongs at the write boundary, not only in the lock client.

long token = lockService.acquire("account:" + accountId).fencingToken();

int updated = jdbc.update("""
    UPDATE accounts
    SET state = ?, fence_token = ?
    WHERE id = ? AND fence_token <= ?
    """, state, token, accountId, token);

if (updated != 1) throw new StaleLockHolderException();

The database performs the comparison and the state change atomically. A request carrying token 41 cannot modify a row after token 42 has been accepted. The token has to be ordered and durable and scoped to the protected resource, and it must not be casually reset when the coordinator restarts. A random lock identifier is useful for safe release but it is not a fence, because randomness establishes identity rather than order. Redis uses random values to avoid deleting another client's lock, and separately recommends fencing for consistency.

Several coordinators expose building blocks for this pattern. Consul increments on acquisition and documents the triple of (Key, LockIndex, Session) as a sequencer that can identify a stale request. ZooKeeper sequential nodes provide monotonically increasing sequence suffixes. etcd exposes creation revisions for election leadership and supports transactionally testing that the leadership revision still matches. The important property is not which coordinator you picked. It is whether the downstream resource actually enforces the ordering information.

Failure modes survive correct acquisition

Correct acquisition can still coexist with unsafe effects. A partition can prevent renewal while leaving access to the protected database intact. A lock server can fail over while an application thread stays paused. A retry can duplicate a side effect that was never idempotent.

A fencing token can be generated correctly and then ignored by one write path. It can be compared without atomicity, or stored only in memory, or reused after a restore, or scoped to the wrong thing. These are protocol failures rather than lock library bugs. Consul makes the advisory nature explicit. Its lock does not itself stop clients from reading or writing the underlying key without ownership.

Some effects cannot naturally enforce fencing. Email delivery, a third-party API, or a legacy device may not expose a conditional operation that rejects a token lower than X. Correctness then has to move to a boundary that can reject duplicates or conflicting state. Idempotency keys can make a retried API request safe when the service supports them, and a database uniqueness constraint can reject a duplicate state transition represented by the same key. A distributed lock cannot retroactively make an unfenceable side effect exclusive.

Testing has to attack stale authority rather than only lock contention. Useful fault injection pauses a holder beyond its TTL. It partitions the holder from the coordinator but not from storage. It delays writes until after reassignment, restarts the coordinator, forces renewal to fail, and reorders retries. The acceptance criterion is stronger than observing that only one lock owner was recorded. The protected resource must reject effects from every superseded epoch. These scenarios follow directly from the documented risks around lease expiration, false failure detection, and delayed execution.

The lock is only half the protocol

Distributed locks are safest when you treat them as advisory coordination plus an explicit mechanism for effect safety. Leases restore liveness by letting ownership expire, but expiration is exactly what creates stale holders. Consensus-backed coordinators improve the authority decision, yet they cannot erase a paused process or a delayed packet. Fencing tokens close that gap only when the protected resource validates them atomically and durably. Where fencing is impossible, something else has to carry the correctness burden, whether that is idempotency, a transaction, or a redesign. The dangerous distributed lock is not the one that occasionally fails to acquire. It is the one that looks successful while obsolete authority can still mutate reality.

items.title: 'Please Let the Internet Die'
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Slashdot reader fjo3 shares an article from Wired: The internet must be put out of its misery. Any rational observer can admit that the current iteration of the web -- and the social fabric woven there -- is not what they signed up for. Symptoms of advanced cultural decay can no longer be ignored. This thing is eating itself. Giants including Meta and Google have been forced to settle massive consumer lawsuits brought over privacy violations and mental health harms allegedly caused by the addictive mechanisms of their platforms. Schools are banning smartphones as multiple countries institute social media restrictions for under-16s. Parents are in a panic about their kids aspiring to careers as social media celebrities, losing themselves in a vast ecosystem of online casinos, or joining extremist movements. Generative AI, briefly considered an amusing novelty, is now a turbocharged slop engine for the web, filling feeds and comment sections with useless, grotesque content. As humans scroll past headlines about AI taking their jobs, confusing fantasy for reality, and contributing to cognitive decline, any consumer appeal the technology might have is turning to anguish. The data centers that power it have become increasingly unpopular, and politically radioactive.
 
To be online, many now admit, is to be endlessly manipulated and exploited. In December, Oxford University Press declared rage bait to be the word of the year, noting that use of the term had tripled over the previous 12 months. The lexical spike represented a heightened awareness that monetized social accounts churn out bad-faith takes and extremist content, automating this abusive behavior with generative AI, simply to profit off hostile engagement. Billionaire oligarchs have opened the floodgates to such inauthentic activity, conspiracy-mongering, and hate speech by rolling back moderation. In short, when you hang around online in 2026, you see little worth saving. Perhaps a decade ago, you felt that the glimmers of community and joy, of artistic and intellectual exchange, were enough to balance out the toxic junk. No longer.

items.title: Hud Launches Agentic Rollouts to Move AI-Written Code From Pull Request to Production
items.author: Kevin John
items.content:
has launched agentic rollouts, a new capability that helps coding agents move a code change from pull request to production while Hud validates each step against how that code actually behaves in live environments. The release targets what has become a major bottleneck in engineering: coding agents write a change in minutes, but that change can wait for days until there is enough confidence to ship it.

With agentic rollouts, Hud analyzes every change before the merge, while the new version takes production traffic, and after the rollout. Safe pull requests can move forward at the pace agents produce them. When a change introduces a regression, Hud catches it, supports rollback or reversion, and hands the coding agent the context it needs to fix the issue and learn from it.

According to Hud, the capability is now available to all its customers.

Three Stages of Validation

Agentic rollouts are built on Hud's runtime code sensor, which teams add through a one-line SDK. The sensor automatically learns how backend code behaves in production at the function level, establishing a baseline that Hud then applies across the entire life of a change.

Before the merge, Hud analyzes the pull request against a production impact map built from real parameters and code flows. It classifies the change by production risk level. When a change is flagged as risky, Hud supplies clear context so the review moves faster. A safe change can ship as fast as the agent wrote it.

Once the new version begins taking traffic, Hud continuously compares its behavior to the established baseline. Regressions surface immediately. Because the analysis runs at the function level, Hud can identify both the root cause and the specific pull request responsible.

If a regression occurs, Hud's context supports rolling back, reverting, and fixing the underlying issue. The coding agent receives deep context on what went wrong so it does not repeat the mistake.

The result is that engineering teams can assess the production impact of changes before, during, and after they ship.

Why the Launch Matters Now

AI is increasingly part of engineers' daily workflows. shows that teams with high AI adoption merge 98% more pull requests, while pull request review time climbs 91%. In practical terms, engineers who lean heavily on AI produce roughly twice as many pull requests, and each one takes about twice as long to review.

The delivery process has not kept up. According to, only 6% of organizations describe their continuous delivery as fully automated.

That combination creates a bottleneck. Agents plan, write, and test code, then open a pull request within minutes. From there, the change waits for a person willing to merge it, because trusting an agent to ship without breaking production is difficult, and the agent has no visibility into how its code runs once deployed. Reviewers may approve pull requests they did not have time to read thoroughly, and someone has to monitor dashboards after each deploy. The more code agents write, the larger that backlog grows. Hud calls this gap the missing link in the AI software factory.

Agentic rollouts are Hud's response to that gap. By validating every step against how the code actually runs in production, Hud aims to bring the speed of shipping closer to the speed of coding.

Riverside Reverts Flawed Deploys in About Eight Minutes

Riverside, the platform for recording and editing studio-quality audio and video, is among the companies running agentic rollouts. The company ships fast with AI, and much of its backend is real-time media code whose true behavior only appears under production load.

Riverside sends every deploy through a canary, combined with Hud's agentic rollout and automatic rollback. According to, flawed deploys are detected quickly and reverted in about eight minutes on average, usually before a customer notices.

Shilo Magen, VP of R&D at Riverside, said: "Our engineers use AI agents every day, and writing code is no longer the bottleneck. The real challenge is shipping that code to production with confidence."

"For a real-time media platform like Riverside, even a small regression can have a major impact on the user experience. With Hud, we can automatically detect regressions and roll back problematic releases in minutes. Our engineers now spend less time worrying about deployments and more time building."

Hud's CEO on Closing the Gap

Roee Adler, Co-Founder and CEO of Hud, framed the launch around the distance between writing code and shipping it.

"AI already changed how code gets written. The bigger problem now is getting that code into production safely, at the speed agents write it. Every engineering leader I talk to is trying to solve this problem. Coding and triage have agents, but the merge and rollout still run on people, because it's scary to give coding agents accountability over the stability and reliability of the production environment. That's the missing link in the AI software factory, and it's the problem we built Hud to solve. With agentic rollouts, agents and engineers work from the same runtime context, at the function level, so a change is merged to production based on evidence. When something does regress, it's immediately detected and fixed, but more importantly the agent that wrote it gets a feedback loop to learn and improve."

That feedback loop reflects the direction Hud is building toward. Each rollout gives the coding agent information about how its changes behave in production, with the aim of reducing risk in subsequent changes.

items.title: What Solana Staking Delegation Teaches Us About AI Agent Authority
items.author: Kenneth Onyebuchi
items.content:
Solana gives you three ways to let someone else act on your funds, and each one grants a different power. A stake authority can point your stake at a validator but can never withdraw it. An SPL Token delegate can send your tokens to any address, up to a cap you set. A liquid staking pool takes your SOL into a program's custody and hands back a token. This piece compares what each model lets a delegate do, what the three have in common, and how the differences decide which one an AI agent that pays for its own compute should get.

What Can a Stake Authority Do?

Every Solana stake account has two authorities defined at creation: a stake authority and a withdraw authority. According to Solana's stake account documentation, the stake authority can delegate the account to a validator, deactivate it, split it, merge it, and assign a new stake authority. It cannot withdraw. The withdraw authority can withdraw undelegated SOL, assign a new withdraw authority, and reset the stake authority, which makes it the authority of last resort.

A stolen stake authority key therefore lets an attacker deactivate your stake or move it between validators, which costs you rewards and time. The SOL stays in the account, and whoever holds the withdraw authority can replace the compromised stake authority.

Marinade Native is a live example of this split. According to Marinade's native staking repository, the user keeps the withdraw authority while Marinade's program holds the stake authority. Marinade can direct the stake, and the owner can take the SOL back without Marinade's cooperation.

What Can an SPL Token Delegate Do?

A Solana token account can name one delegate and an allowance. Solana's spend permissions documentation describes the result: the delegate can transfer tokens out of the account up to the approved amount, and each transfer reduces the remaining allowance. The SPL Token program documentation adds that a delegate may transfer or burn up to the amount it was delegated, and it names that amount as the delegate's only limit, so the approval does not fix a destination. An account holds one active delegate at a time, and the owner's revoke instruction removes all of its permissions at once.

This is a different power from a stake authority. A stake authority has no path to move funds to an address of its choosing, and an SPL delegate has exactly that, bounded by the cap. If a delegate key is stolen, the most an attacker can take is the remaining allowance. The cap is the whole safety mechanism, which makes its size the main design decision.

Neither page describes an expiry. The documented ways an approval ends are revocation and the allowance reaching zero, so a time limit has to come from the owner revoking the approval or from a layer built on top of the token program.

What Changes in a Liquid Staking Pool?

Liquid staking moves custody. In Jito's design, depositors send SOL to a pool built on the SPL stake pool program, which holds the stake accounts and issues JitoSOL in return. Marinade Liquid runs on its own program rather than the SPL one and issues mSOL. In both pools the holder receives a claim token and no longer controls the authorities on any stake account.

Exit works differently too. The owner of a stake account or a token allowance can cut off the delegate with one transaction. A pool holder leaves by redeeming or selling the token, which depends on the pool's liquidity and on the program continuing to behave as written. The trust sits in the code and in whoever can change it. Marinade's contract addresses page lists the Liquid program's upgrade authority as a 6-of-13 multisig.

What Do the Three Models Share?

Three properties hold across all of them:

  • The owner's key stays the authority of last resort. The withdraw authority can reset the stake authority, a token owner can revoke or replace a delegate, and a pool holder keeps the right to redeem.
  • The delegate's powers form a fixed list that the runtime or program enforces on every transaction.
  • The damage from a compromised delegate is bounded by what it was granted.

That third property is where the models diverge. A stake authority costs you rewards, an SPL delegate costs you the remaining allowance, and a pool's upgrade authority can reach every deposit in the pool.

Delegate, deactivate, split, merge

Transfer or burn up to the allowance

Hold stake accounts, issue a pool token

Can it move funds to any address?

Only as the program's code allows

Worst case if the key is stolen

Depends on the program and its upgrade authority

Reset the stake authority with the withdraw key

Redeem or sell the pool token

Does Delegating Stake Carry Risk?

Delegating to a validator has not put principal at risk on Solana so far, because slashing is not live on the network. According to Everstake's overview, proposals to add it are still under discussion: SIMD-0204 would record evidence of slashable behavior and SIMD-0212 would set the penalties, which are not finalized. If slashing ships, a stake authority that picks a misbehaving validator could cost the owner part of the principal in addition to rewards, and the maximum loss for that model would no longer be rewards alone.

Scale is easy to overstate, so here are the dated figures. DefiLlama lists Jito at about $1.108 billion in total value locked as of October 16, 2026, and Marinade at about $763 million as of October 17, 2026, roughly $1.87 billion combined. Marinade's figure combines its Native, Liquid, and Select products, and the Native portion stays in accounts whose withdraw authority belongs to users. Total value locked measures how much money relies on each design. It makes no statement about incident history, and I make no safety claim from it.

Pick the narrowest primitive that matches the verb the agent needs:

  • If the agent manages existing stake, such as choosing validators for a treasury, a stake authority gives it direction and no withdrawal power.
  • If the agent pays invoices, such as a GPU marketplace bill, an SPL Token delegate with a cap sized to a billing period gives it spending power with a known maximum loss.
  • If the agent needs a position that stays liquid, a pool token works, and the trust moves to the pool program and its upgrade authority.

The spending case is the one most agent builders face first. Suppose an agent rents GPUs at $2 an hour and expects 40 hours of work a week. A weekly cap of $80 in a stablecoin means a leaked key costs at most $80 before the owner revokes it. A raw API key with no cap has no such number, which is the problem I described in an API key is not delegated authority. Because the base approval has no expiry, the owner also needs a routine that revokes or reduces the allowance at the end of each period.

The stake authority is the best fit when an agent should never be able to move funds at all. A pool is the weakest fit for an agent that pays bills, because spending from a pool means redeeming first and the agent's risk then includes the pool's code.

The useful question for an agent on Solana is which verb it needs, because each delegation model grants a different one. Size the grant to the loss you can absorb if the key leaks, and write that number down before you deploy. If you are building agent payments, start with an SPL Token delegate and a cap, then tell me in the comments what cap you would set for a week of GPU rental.

items.title: Pluto Security Uncovers Self-Iterating Cryptominer Campaign Hidden in Hugging Face AI Models
items.author: Kevin John
items.content:
A financially motivated operator or small group has been using the since September 2026 to distribute cryptocurrency miners and backdoors disguised as small Qwen2 language models, according to a report shared by. The campaign has run through two waves and more than 40 code iterations across 28 repositories. Its second wave remained live as of October 25, five days after Pluto Security reported it. Downloads across the campaign and its linked models had passed 21,000 by that date.

Pluto Security reported the first wave to Hugging Face and ModelScope. Both Hugging Face accounts behind that wave and a ModelScope mirror were taken down. Within days, a second wave appeared under four new accounts, with revised loaders and reverse shells in place of the first wave's hardcoded SSH key. A header comment in the wave-two payload references "report §9.1" and states that "ammunition must be self-hosted."

The campaign spans 28 repositories across six Hugging Face accounts and a ModelScope mirror. Counting seven linked repositories that share technique without proven shared ownership, the total reaches 35. According to Pluto Security's October 25 findings, downloads break down as 18,544 on the 16 live second-wave repositories, 2,342 on the linked models, and 728 recorded on the first wave before removal, for 21,614 in all.

A single repository, , accounts for about 97% of second-wave downloads. It stood at 7,354 downloads on October 20, when Pluto Security disclosed it, reached 9,584 within hours, and was listed at 18,012 on October 25.

The payload rides on a. When a user loads a model with trust_remote_code=True, an auto_map entry in the repository's config.json tells Transformers to download and import a Python file from the repository. That code runs with the caller's privileges during model loading, so no malicious weights are needed. The flagship's model.safetensors is a 42-byte file containing no tensors.

Those checks did not flag the malicious Python loader files identified in Pluto Security's investigation. In its tests, modeling_evil2.py in qwen2-tiny came back safe from every scanner that ran, with JFrog reporting it was not a machine-learning model. None of the 12 first-wave repositories were flagged.

The places responsibility on the user, advising developers to "always verify the content of the modeling files when using this argument."

Still Live, and Still Earning

The campaign grew from a 37-line SSH backdoor to a 305-line fileless miner in three weeks, then was rebuilt after the takedown with reverse shells and more varied payloads.

Pluto Security also traced mining proceeds. The first-wave payout wallet was still active on public pool dashboards on October 21, long after its repositories were removed. According to the researchers, it had received about 2,276 PRL, valued at roughly $5,000 at the time, across 716 transactions and sent about 2,241 PRL onward.

Two live workers reported PeakMiner, the same mining client Pluto Security recovered from the second-wave binary. While Pluto Security analyzed the wallet, nine workers named like a shared notebook cluster joined within 90 seconds of each other and stopped submitting shares about six minutes later, consistent with an administrator terminating the jobs.

The miner launches fileless from memory using memfd_create and runs as a process disguised as a kernel worker, . Earlier builds also throttled the miner to stay under monitoring thresholds. The binary is hosted in the repositories, with mirror fallbacks.

The syscore.bin file is 33.8 MB in wave one and 40.6 MB in wave two, where it is packed with UPX and two packer markers were altered from UPX! to PEK! so that upx -d rejects the file. Pluto Security restored both markers and unpacked it to reveal peakminer.

Persistence goes deep. Early builds planted an ed25519 SSH key in six paths, including the xinference user's home. Payloads also add shell-startup hooks in /root/.bashrc, /root/.profile and ~/.bashrc, a watchdog at /tmp/.cch/svc.py that restarts a missing miner every 120 seconds, and, in wave one, cron persistence.

Three wave-two builds open a reconnecting reverse shell to 212.32.253.3 on port 443 or 9443 before mining. The r1r13 payload performs GPU platform discovery for LLaMA-Factory deployments and collects Tencent Cloud metadata, with exfiltration to 2.28.9.199:7000. The wave-one command-and-control server, 8.137.187.63, sits on Alibaba Cloud.

Pluto Security's assessment points to a financially motivated, Chinese-speaking operator or small group. Wave-one code carries comments in Simplified Chinese such as "daemon disguise name," "blend into Xinference directory" and "kill rival processes."

The command-and-control runs on Alibaba Cloud, the miner binary is mirrored on ModelScope and hf-mirror.com, the targeting assumes Xinference and Tencent Cloud, and activity clusters between 18:38 and 21:19 UTC, which is late night in China Standard Time.

One wave-two line, the soumikmahato "parasit" build, carries Indonesian-language comments and a different build system. Pluto Security says that fits either a second operator in the same niche or one operator running a deliberately different-looking line for redundancy.

Pluto Security advises reviewing the .py files an auto_map points to before setting trust_remote_code, pinning the reviewed revision, and running untrusted code with limited privileges, restricted network access and no production secrets.

Teams that loaded one of the listed models should check hosts for /tmp/.cch/, unexpected svc.py processes, and a process named carrying mining arguments, and inspect Xinference registrations for encoded qwen2-tiny- or ezv- names.

Cleaning the miner is not enough, because killing it or deleting the model does not remove persistence. Tokens, cloud credentials, passwords, and SSH keys the compromised process could reach should be rotated from a clean machine.

Pluto Security also notes that a static check at upload time for subprocess, socket, ctypes or raw-IP network calls in files referenced by could have caught these payloads earlier.

items.title: Google Struggling to Make AI Mode Searches Pay
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Alphabet shares fell nearly 10% after Google disclosed that searches through its AI Mode generate less revenue than traditional search, even as overall search revenue grew 12% year over year to $63.25 billion. The Register reports: Alphabet on Wednesday reported its Q3 results, which included news that its year-over-year search query growth rate is the highest it's been in the last five years. Some of that growth comes from users adopting "AI Mode" -- Google's latest LLM-powered search system. Google's revenue from search rose 12 percent year-over-year to $63.25 billion, a little lower than the 14.5 percent growth the company reported in last year's Q3.
 
During Alphabet's earnings call, chief business officer Philipp Schindler said the slowdown was caused by "lower monetization we were seeing in AI Mode." That's a worry given that Google is spending enormous sums on infrastructure. $51.4 billion went out the door in Q3, around two thirds of it going towards servers and networking equipment. The rest funded datacenter builds. That spending appears to have impacted profitability, as Alphabet reported $26.17 billion net income for the quarter. Last year's Q3, during which Google revenue was $102.35 billion, produced $35 billion net income.
 
Schindler argued that AI search will pay off. "On AI Mode, many of these queries are upper funnel queries, allowing us to capture new, high-value commercial intent," he told investors. "In addition, the majority of AI Mode queries are incremental, creating more monetization opportunities over time." Google tried to seize one of those opportunities today, by turning on ads alongside AI Mode searches around the world, after first testing them in the US only. But for now, AI Mode searches aren't as lucrative as Google's existing search business, which brought in just under half of Alphabet's $125.8 billion quarterly revenue.

items.title: Ink Droplets In Motion Snag Top Prize In Nikon Small World Contest
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
A 25-year-old German photographer won the 2026 Nikon Small World competition with a microscopic image freezing ink droplets in midair as an inkjet printer deposits them onto paper. Ars Technica reports that Ole Bielfeldt "beat out 1,802 other entries hailing from 69 different countries." From the report: Bielfeldt became interested in photomicrography during the COVID-19 lockdown after discovering an old microscope in his parents' attic. He figured out how to build an adaptor out of a tube and some wood to connect the microscope to his father's camera and taught himself the art through trial and error, building custom tools as needed. He documents how he captures transformative images of everyday objects with behind-the-scenes videos posted to macrofying, his photography and videography brand.
 
It was Bielfeldt's curiosity about the inner workings of inkjet printers that inspired his winning entry, but capturing the action of ink drops being deposited on paper was a challenge, given that the process happens so quickly. The droplets, for instance, moved faster than the camera's shutter speed. Bielfeldt's solution was to deconstruct the printer so that the paper moved under a stationary (rather than moving) printhead, and then take the image in a dark room, using a flash to serve as the shutter, thereby freezing the ink drops mid-air. There was no need for pricey equipment. Bielfeldt does not use AI in his images, preferring to rely on traditional techniques. "Ole Bielfeldt's winning image embodies what makes Nikon Small World so powerful: the intersection of microscope imaging, ingenuity, and artistry," said Eric Flem, a spokesperson for Nikon Instruments. "By using a microscope objective in a different way, he transformed a familiar object into something altogether new and previously unseen. It is a reminder that the microscope is not only a scientific tool but also a creative one, capable of expanding how we see and imagine the world around us."
